Here's the layout comparison. Three columns: the payload as it stands today (= vc-x1, since we're byte-identical to it), iiac-perf as it stands on the bookmark, and my suggestion.

| Payload / vc-x1 today | iiac-perf today | Suggested |
|---|---|---|
| `CLAUDE.md` (2 imports) | `CLAUDE.md` (1 import) | `CLAUDE.md` (1 import: `@AGENTS.md`) |
| `AGENTS.md` | `AGENTS.md` | `AGENTS.md` (pinned) |
| `custom.md` (skeleton w/ placeholders) | `custom.md` (generic stub) | `custom.md` (generic stub, ships from payload) |
| - | `custom-family.md` | `custom-family.md` (member-only; not in payload) |
| `agent-data/cycle-checklists.md` | `agent-data/cycle.md` | `agent-data/cycle-checklists.md` (see naming note) |
| `agent-data/cycle-protocol.md` | `notes/cycle-protocol.md` | `agent-data/cycle-protocol.md` (pinned) |
| `agent-data/versioning.md` | `notes/versioning.md` | `agent-data/versioning.md` (pinned) |
| `agent-data/jj.md` | `agent-data/jj.md` | `agent-data/jj.md` |
| `agent-data/prose.md` | `agent-data/prose.md` | `agent-data/prose.md` |
| `agent-data/notes.md` | `agent-data/notes.md` | `agent-data/notes.md` |
| `agent-data/code.md` | `agent-data/code.md` | `agent-data/code.md` |

As a tree, the suggested layout with each file's role:

```
<project>/
|-- CLAUDE.md            shim: one line, @AGENTS.md; payload-identical everywhere
|-- AGENTS.md            pinned: hard rules, terminology, file map, change process
|-- custom.md            never-pinned by content, but payload-identical for a member:
|                        generic stub + the one pointer line "Read ./custom-family.md."
|-- custom-family.md     member-only: medium/validation, membership, messaging, dogfood log
|                        (a non-member project has no pointer line and no file)
`-- agent-data/          pinned satellites, read at the moment of action
    |-- cycle-checklists.md   condensed checklists: commit / push / open / close-out
    |-- cycle-protocol.md     full protocol + rationale; wins over any checklist summary
    |-- versioning.md         scheme, suffix, advancement, version-of-record
    |-- jj.md                 jj usage, revsets, ochid, bookmarks (create/land)
    |-- prose.md              prose form, punctuation, title identity
    |-- notes.md              TODO / chores / done mechanics
    `-- code.md               doc comments, unwrap discipline
```

Reading order at a session: harness auto-loads `CLAUDE.md` -> `AGENTS.md`; rule 0 sends the session to `custom.md`; its pointer line (members only) sends it to `custom-family.md`; the `agent-data/` files are read per-action, not at acquaint.

**The naming note - I've changed my lean.** Last message I mildly preferred renaming `cycle-checklists.md` to `cycle.md`. Settling the file-set question changes the calculus: once `cycle-protocol.md` moves into `agent-data/` and the two sit side by side, the pair `cycle.md` + `cycle-protocol.md` reads backwards - `cycle.md` sounds like the primary file, but the protocol is what wins on disagreement. The pair `cycle-checklists.md` + `cycle-protocol.md` is self-describing: which is the condensation and which is the authority is visible in the names. The new rule-ish sections that made me like `cycle.md` (cycles-run-on-a-bookmark, topic-bookmarks-are-drafts) are, on a closer read, summaries whose full statements live in the protocol, so "checklists" is still an honest name. Cost asymmetry supports this too: keeping `cycle-checklists.md` costs vc-x1 nothing and iiac-perf one rename they'd do anyway during their baseline sync; renaming to `cycle.md` costs vc-x1 a rename plus fixing the anchor links in hard rules 1, 2, 3, and 7.

Two smaller naming thoughts while we're here:

- **`custom-family.md`**: the name is iiac-perf's and I'd keep it - it reads naturally as "the family part of custom" and sorts beside `custom.md` in a listing. Alternatives like `family.md` or `member.md` lose that adjacency.
- **Not in the set, for completeness**: `jj-tips.md` (hosted once in the template repo, not copied to members), the template's `messages/` + `MESSAGES.md` (community infrastructure), and `notes/` (project records). Nothing about the proposal changes those.

**The plain version:** the two repos already agree on seven of the files; the whole layout dispute is really three decisions - the two protocol-ish files move back into the pinned `agent-data/` directory (iiac-perf keeps them in `notes/`), the checklist file keeps its longer name `cycle-checklists.md` (I've reversed my earlier lean, because next to `cycle-protocol.md` the short name would misleadingly sound like the boss file), and everyone adopts the stub `custom.md` + member-only `custom-family.md` split.

content.content:
1	# Cycle protocol
2	
3	This protocol uses [Prose form](prose.md#prose-form). It
4	contains instructions on how a commit cycle is accomplished.
5	
6	Universal file, pinned to the template repository; do not edit
7	here. Project overrides go in [custom.md](../custom.md).
8	
9	The artifact a cycle produces is whatever the bot generates from
10	the conversation: code, prose, an image, a song, a screenplay.
11	The steps below use a Rust crate as the running example (the
12	cargo cycle, `Cargo.toml` versioning); substitute your medium's
13	equivalents. This project's manifest is recorded in
14	[versioning.md](versioning.md).
15	
16	## Cycles
17	
18	A cycle has three phases:
19	
20	- **[Preparation](#preparation)** (`X.Y.Z-0`): the cycle's
21	  first commit, when it needs setup (a lightweight cycle omits
22	  it and starts at `-1`; see
23	  [versioning.md](versioning.md#step-numbering)). Sets up the
24	  cycle:
25	  - Bump the version-of-record to `X.Y.Z-0` (where it lives
26	    and the suffix scheme are project-specific; see
27	    [versioning.md](versioning.md)).
28	  - Pick up a `## Todo` item (typically the top-ranked,
29	    #1) into `## In Progress` (bold title + succinct problem
30	    statement + plan ladder).
31	  - Open the [chores section](#chores-sections).
32	- **[Work-N](#work-n)** (`X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...): the
33	  commits that implement the change. As many as the change
34	  needs; each runs through the
35	  [per-commit flow](#per-commit-flow).
36	- **[Close-out](#close-out)** (bare `X.Y.Z`): the cycle's
37	  last commit. Bookkeeping only:
38	  - Move the picked-up item to a one-line entry in
39	    `## Done`.
40	  - Move the `## In Progress` block into the
41	    [chores section](#chores-sections).
42	  - Optionally update `notes/README.md` if functionality
43	    changed.
44	
45	A cycle's commits are published to the project remote
46	either incrementally or as one batch at close-out; the
47	result must always be published at close-out. See
48	[Pushing](#pushing).
49	
50	**Sub-cycles.** When a Work commit's scope grows enough to
51	warrant its own ladder, it subdivides: `X.Y.Z-3.0`
52	Preparation, `X.Y.Z-3.1` / `X.Y.Z-3.2` Work, `X.Y.Z-3`
53	Close-out. The same three-phase shape applies recursively
54	at every depth. See [Numbering](#numbering) for the
55	suffix rule and [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders)
56	for the local-ladder mechanics.
57	
58	## Chores sections
59	
60	A **chores section** is a `##` section in `notes/chores/chores-NN.md` recording landed work.
61	In general, every commit that lands on the permanent branch should have a rung in some
62	section's as-built ladder in a chores file.
63	
64	The phrase **"Open" the chores section** means append a `##` header to the current
65	`notes/chores/chores-NN.md` with the title it records (e.g. `## refactor: foo bar`), add the
66	file's `## Table of Contents` entry, and start the **as-built ladder**: one
67	`- [[N]] X.Y.Z[-n] <title>` rung per commit the section records, each opening with the literal
68	`[[N]]` placeholder. **Each work commit then appends its own rung + narrative note as it
69	lands**, so the chores record is built up per commit, not held back and written all at once at
70	close-out; close-out only *finalizes* (title sync, design subsections, retiring the
71	`## In Progress` block). Rung placeholders are backfilled later, once their commits are
72	permanent (see [Commits backfill](#commits-backfill) below).
73	
74	Fuller chores conventions (content rules, header sync, design subsection pattern, ladder and
75	reference formatting, the Table of Contents) live in
76	[Chores conventions](notes.md#chores-conventions).
77	
78	### Commits backfill
79	
80	An as-built ladder rung cites its commit by SHA, but a SHA isn't stable until the commit lands
81	on a **permanent branch** (`main`, or a long-lived release/patch branch that won't be
82	rewritten); a rebase or squash rewrites it on the way. So:
83	
84	- A rung is **written with the literal `[[N]]` placeholder**.
85	- **Backfill once the commit is on a permanent branch**, where its SHA is final. A commit
86	  can't record its own SHA (that would change the hash), so the fill always lands one push
87	  later: **each push backfills the rungs of the commits the previous push made permanent.** On
88	  a topic branch the sections instead wait until the branch lands, so no SHA is ever written
89	  that a later rebase could invalidate.
90	- A deliberate rewrite of already-recorded commits (a coordinated re-describe, a retroactive
91	  reshape) invalidates their recorded SHAs. Re-record them once the rewrite is published, on
92	  the same one-push-later timing.
93	
94	Each rung carries its own `[N]` ref, with the commit URL + 40-hex SHA in the file's
95	`# References` (format in
96	[Chores commit references](notes.md#chores-commit-references)). A section's `##`
97	title matches its close-out commit title, and each rung's text its own commit title, so a rare
98	deliberate rewrite of a permanent-branch commit re-syncs via `git log --grep "<title>"`.
99	Sections that predate the ladder form keep their grandfathered `Commits:` lines.
100	
101	The per-push cadence is a project choice, not dogma. A **per-close-out** model (recording a
102	cycle's SHAs at its close-out) is equally valid. The one invariant: a recorded SHA must be
103	permanent.
104	
105	## Preparation
106	
107	The cycle's first commit (`X.Y.Z-0`), when the cycle needs
108	setup (a lightweight cycle omits it; see
109	[versioning.md](versioning.md#step-numbering)):
110	
111	- **Bump the version-of-record** to `X.Y.Z-0`. Where it
112	  lives, the suffix scheme, and any derived files (a
113	  lockfile, a sourced manifest version) are
114	  project-specific; see [versioning.md](versioning.md).
115	- **Move a `## Todo` item** (if the cycle has one) into
116	  `## In Progress` and the todo item should have:
117	  - A **bold title line**, which will be the chores
118	    section header, minus the `## ` prefix.
119	  - A **succinct problem statement**; add if one is needed
120	  - A **plan ladder**.
121	- **Open the [chores section](#chores-sections)**: append a
122	  `##` header with the title it records, the cycle's
123	  anticipated close-out title.
124	
125	## Work-N
126	
127	The cycle's work commits (`X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...)
128	implement the change. As many as needed:
129	
130	- Each commit runs through the
131	  **[per-commit flow](#per-commit-flow)**.
132	- **Interim pushes** are optional (backup, progress
133	  visibility).
134	- Close-out is the only mandatory push (see
135	  [Pushing](#pushing)).
136	- **Subdivide into a sub-cycle** if a Work commit's
137	  scope grows enough (see
138	  [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders)).
139	
140	## Close-out
141	
142	The cycle's last commit (bare `X.Y.Z`) does bookkeeping
143	only, and the commit body describes that bookkeeping, not
144	what happens post-squash:
145	
146	- **Move the picked-up item** from `## In Progress` to a
147	  one-line entry (with a chores `[N]` ref) in `## Done`.
148	- **Finalize the chores section** (opened during Preparation
149	  and grown per commit; see [Chores sections](#chores-sections)):
150	  - The problem statement is already the chores intro (written
151	    when the section was opened) and the plan ladder is already
152	    the `### As-built ladder` (a rung appended per commit), so
153	    close-out only *finalizes*, it does not cut-and-paste.
154	  - Sync the chores header to the **final** commit title if the
155	    cycle's scope shifted; update every anchor back-reference.
156	  - Add any `### design subsections`; optional `### Outcome`
157	    notes.
158	  - Replace the `## In Progress` cycle block with
159	    `_No cycle currently in progress._`. Under a multi-cycle
160	    program (program `###`, current stage `####`) this retires
161	    the stage `####` only; the program heading and its ladder
162	    stay, the shipped rung flipped `(done)`, so the marker
163	    sits inside the program block until the next stage is
164	    picked up.
165	- **Update `notes/README.md`** if functionality changed
166	  (new flags, new subcommands, changed behavior).
167	
168	Whether to **squash** the cycle into one commit before the
169	publishing push, or push as-is, is decided at push time; see
170	[Pushing](#pushing).
171	
172	## Numbering
173	
174	Each commit's phase is encoded in the version suffix: `-0`
175	Preparation, `-1`/`-2`/... Work, bare `X.Y.Z` Close-out,
176	recursively for sub-cycles. The full scheme (disambiguation,
177	nesting, optional Preparation, the project's version-of-record
178	format, and the per-phase bump) lives in
179	[versioning.md](versioning.md#step-numbering), which is the
180	single source of truth for this repo's versioning.
181	
182	## Per-commit flow
183	
184	Every commit (Preparation, each Work commit, Close-out) goes
185	through:
186	
187	1. **Mark this commit `(current)`** as the first edit in
188	   `TODO.md > ## In Progress` (`TODO.md` is at the repo
189	   root).
190	2. **Do the work** (see [Iterative work](#iterative-work)
191	   for the loop-and-squash technique).
192	3. **Flip this commit `(current)` -> `(done)`** in `## In
193	   Progress`, before the cargo cycle and the commit.
194	4. **Validate the artifact**, a medium-specific step, skip-able
195	   for notes-only commits, mandatory at close-out. For the Rust
196	   example the cargo cycle is:
197	   1. `cargo fmt`
198	   2. `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`
199	   3. `cargo test`
200	   4. `cargo install --path . --locked`
201	   5. (re-test if anything substantive changed)
202	5. **Work review.** Stop *before* writing any description;
203	   tell the user "ready to commit." The user reviews the
204	   changes and we iterate until complete.
205	6. **Write the commit description**; see
206	   [Commit description](#commit-description).
207	7. **Commit Description review.** Show the title + body
208	   and stop. The user reviews the description. Iterate.
209	8. **Commit + push.** Hand the approved title/body to
210	   `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "..." --body "..."`, whose
211	   commit stages commit both repos and stamp the `ochid:`
212	   trailers. Never pre-commit the rung with `jj commit`: an
213	   empty `@` at push mints a stamped empty duplicate
214	   (bugs.md #6). Push approval is per-push, so step 7's
215	   review covers it only when the user's go explicitly
216	   includes the push.
217	
218	**Two overrides apply:**
219	
220	- **Deviation or question.** Any time the work deviates
221	  from the agreed plan, or a question arises, stop and
222	  surface it; don't push through.
223	- **ESC-ESC.** The user can interrupt at any point to pull
224	  a review or question forward.
225	
226	## Commit description
227	
228	[Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/):
229	
230	```
231	<type>: <short description>
232	<type>(scope): <short description>   # optional scope
233	```
234	
235	Titles carry **no trailing `(<version>)` suffix**. The
236	version-of-record (where it lives and its bump cadence, see
237	[versioning.md](versioning.md)) is useful for confirming
238	you're running the version you're testing, not a per-commit
239	title marker. We think per-commit version-in-title is
240	unstable on large projects: many changes are in flight
241	simultaneously, and a version is only stable once merged into
242	the main repo, so titles don't carry one.
243	
244	### Title
245	
246	- <=72 chars total.
247	- Common types: `feat`, `fix`, `refactor`, `test`,
248	  `docs`, `chore`; optional `(scope)` in parentheses after
249	  the type, per the spec.
250	- Favor terse phrasings.
251	- **Distinct per step.** Each of a cycle's commits gets its
252	  own descriptive title (no shared cycle title with a step
253	  marker). Share a greppable stem across the cycle's titles
254	  (e.g. `ring buffer`) so `git log --grep` collects them; the
255	  chores section header matches the close-out title. See
256	  [Conventional-commit shape](prose.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit).
257	
258	### Body
259	
260	[Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) (intro + bullets),
261	wrap ≤72. Bullet content differs per repo:
262	
263	- **Work-repo body**: file-by-file. One bullet per file
264	  changed (file plus a one-line gist), in short sentence
265	  fragments (full sentences are discouraged). Sub-bullets
266	  for files with multiple distinct changes:
267	
268	  ```
269	  - path/to/file1
270	    - first distinct change
271	    - second distinct change, wrapping to next line
272	       with continuation indented 5
273	  ```
274	
275	  The list **opens with the version bump** as its first
276	  bullet, for the Rust example
277	  `- Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock: vX.Y.Z-xxxx` (generally:
278	  the medium's version-of-record files); `-xxxx` stands for
279	  the whole suffix, nested or not (`v0.78.0-1`,
280	  `v0.78.0-3.1`), per
281	  [versioning.md](versioning.md#grammar-and-storage). Titles stay
282	  version-free (above), so this first bullet is the
283	  version's durable, visible home, and log viewers (e.g.
284	  gitk's message pane) show it without opening the commit's
285	  file list. Adopted 2026-07-24.
286	
287	  The file-by-file list is the source of truth for the
288	  cycle's mechanical change record. Chores carries the
289	  narrative + design, not a copy of it. Promote any
290	  "why" beyond one sentence to a chores `###` subsection.
291	
292	- **Bot-repo (`.claude`) body**: bullets describe
293	  in-session activity rather than work-repo changes.
294	
295	### Trailer
296	
297	`ochid:` as the last line of the body; see
298	[Cross-repo linking (ochid trailers)](jj.md#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)
299	in agent-data/jj.md for the convention.
300	
301	For breaking changes, use the hyphenated `BREAKING-CHANGE:`
302	trailer key. `BREAKING CHANGE:` (with a space) is the only
303	space-separated key the Conventional Commits spec allows; the
304	hyphenated form is also valid and avoids the space ambiguity.
305	
306	## Reviewing changes
307	
308	Work review looks at the **uncommitted working-copy diff**,
309	on the way to commit. The user opens diffs in their
310	editor (Zed, VSCode); jj commands are for terminal:
311	
312	- `jj diff`: working-copy diff (uncommitted)
313	- `jj diff -r @-`: diff of the previous commit
314	- `jj diff --from <X> --to <Y>`: any two revisions
315	- `jj show -r <X>`: description + diff for one rev
316	
317	Don't `jj edit -r @-` to view a past commit, because that marks
318	it mutable and shifts `@`; use `jj diff -r @-` or
319	`jj show -r @-`.
320	
321	No preflight while a review iterates: `fmt` / `clippy` / `test`
322	wait until the review settles, since `fmt` mutates files in ways
323	that interact badly with the user's mid-review edits. Validation
324	runs once, on the settled state, per the per-commit checklist.
325	
326	See [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders) for the
327	close-out squash recipe and recovery; revset primitives
328	are in [`jj.md > Revsets`](jj.md#revsets).
329	
330	## Pushing
331	
332	### Policy
333	
334	Push is **discretionary** during the cycle (backup,
335	progress visibility) and **mandatory at close-out**, since
336	the cycle's result must be published.
337	
338	**Approval is per-push.** Every push (any repo, any kind:
339	cycle push, interim backup, recovery/surgery force-push)
340	happens only after the user has reviewed the changes to be
341	published and explicitly approved that specific push.
342	Approval of a plan that *includes* a push does not authorize
343	the push itself; stop and ask again at the moment of pushing.
344	
345	**Default is interactive; an explicit scoped delegation waives
346	the gates.** The gates above (per-push approval, the
347	commit-description review that shows title+body and stops, and
348	the hard stop after push/squash-push) are the *interactive
349	default*.
350	They yield when the user **explicitly** delegates a complete,
351	bounded task and authorizes carrying it through ("do all of X
352	and push each step, don't check in"). The bot then proceeds
353	through that task's commits and pushes without stopping, and
354	continues past each push to the next step. Conditions:
355	
356	- **Explicit grant.** Never inferred from a task merely being
357	  well-scoped; the user's words must authorize unattended
358	  completion. "Commit and push" (or "then push") names the
359	  destination, not a waiver: it authorizes the push *after*
360	  the normal work review and description review, not skipping
361	  them. Only wording that explicitly waives the stops ("don't
362	  check in", "no need to review", "carry it through
363	  unattended") waives them.
364	- **Bounded goal.** Covers the named task only; does not carry
365	  to the next task or a vaguer follow-on.
366	- **Destructive ops still pause.** Delegation covers the task's
367	  ordinary commits and pushes; it does *not* pre-authorize a
368	  genuinely irreversible action (force-push over published
369	  history, history rewrite, deleting a remote branch). Those can
370	  permanently destroy work and aren't a normal cycle step, so the
371	  bot flags one before acting. An ordinary delegated cycle never
372	  reaches this.
373	- **Still transparent.** Report each commit/push as it lands
374	  (title + outcome) so the user can catch up.
375	- **When in doubt, ask.** Ambiguous authorization falls back to
376	  per-push approval.
377	
378	### Shape at close-out push
379	
380	At close-out the cycle's *work* is done; its *published
381	shape* is the remaining choice, made at push time. Surface
382	the options and get user approval before pushing. Once on
383	the target, changing shape is a remote rewrite (force-push,
384	needs approval), so choose deliberately.
385	
386	- **Squash to one commit**: single entry on the target.
387	  Right for straightforward changes where the Work-N is
388	  focused on one or two files.
389	- **Trapezoid** (a `git merge --no-ff` merge commit)
390	  *(current default)*: the target gains a merge commit
391	  (`X.Y.Z`) whose first parent is the trunk line and whose
392	  second parent is the cycle's ladder, so
393	  `git log --first-parent` reads one commit per cycle while
394	  every rung stays reachable. See
395	  [Trapezoid close-out recipe](#trapezoid-close-out-recipe)
396	  for the full sequence.
397	- **Keep separate**: one commit per cycle entry on
398	  `main`. Use when the decomposition itself is
399	  informative. Each chores section keeps its own header /
400	  ladder refs; no consolidation churn.
401	
402	A squash is set up before invoking `vc-x1 push`; a trapezoid
403	is reshaped between two pushes (the recipe below). For any
404	other shape, drive `jj git push` directly.
405	
406	### Trapezoid close-out recipe
407	
408	A [trapezoid](#shape-at-close-out-push) close-out is
409	published in four steps: an ordinary close-out push, a
410	two-command reshape, and a second push that re-points the
411	bookmark at the reshaped commit.
412	
413	```
414	  main line   ...──<base>──────────────────<closeout>──
415	                      \                    /
416	  ladder             <rung-1>──...──<tip>─┘
417	```
418	
419	- `<base>`: the **parent of the ladder's first rung**, which
420	  is the trunk position when the cycle opened. It becomes the
421	  first parent.
422	- `<tip>`: the cycle's last Work commit. It becomes the
423	  second parent.
424	- `<closeout>`: the close-out commit, created by step 1.
425	
426	The steps. Only step 1 is a `vc-x1 push`; the rest is jj,
427	because after step 1 the commits already exist and all that
428	remains is reshaping and publishing them:
429	
430	1. `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "..." --body "..."`
431	   - the ordinary close-out push. It commits both repos, stamps the
432	   `ochid:` trailers, and publishes `<closeout>` linearly.
433	2. `jj rebase -r <closeout> --onto <base> --onto <tip>`
434	   - `<closeout>` becomes the merge. Parent order is the
435	   argument order.
436	3. `jj new <closeout>`
437	   -  puts an empty `@` above the merge.
438	4. `jj git push --bookmark <bookmark> -R .`
439	   - publishes the reshaped commit. The bookmark needs no `jj bookmark set`:
440	   it follows the rewrite in step 2 automatically. The bot
441	   repo is untouched, and its session tail goes out with a
442	   separate `vc-x1 squash-push` afterwards.
443	
444	**Step 4 is not a `vc-x1 push`** (corrected at the `0.77.0`
445	close-out, which tried it). Push runs its whole pipeline or
446	none of it, and the bot repo is never quiet for long: by the
447	time the reshape is done, `.claude` holds the session writes
448	from steps 1-3, so `commit-bot` wants to run and the message
449	stage demands a title for it. The result is a bot-side
450	requirement blocking a work-side publish that needs nothing
451	but a moved ref. Publishing an already-made commit is a
452	different operation from committing and publishing, and only
453	the latter is push's job.
454	
455	#### Details
456	
457	- **Verify two parents before step 4.** `jj log -r <closeout>
458	  -T 'parents.map(|p| p.change_id().short(8))'` must list
459	  both. jj preserves the second parent even though `<base>`
460	  is an ancestor of `<tip>` (observed at `0.74.0`, `0.75.0`,
461	  `0.76.0`), but a collapsed merge is indistinguishable from
462	  a correct one in `jj log --no-graph` and is only visible
463	  once published.
464	- **`<base>` is not always the previous close-out.** A docs
465	  or planning interlude between cycles sits on the trunk line
466	  and must stay there; take the parent of the ladder's first
467	  rung, not the last close-out.
468	- **Step 3 is about `@`, not the bookmark.** The bookmark
469	  follows the rewrite in step 2 on its own. What step 2
470	  leaves misplaced is the working copy: `jj rebase -r`
471	  re-parents descendants onto the rebased commit's **old**
472	  parent, so the empty `@` from step 1 lands beside the merge
473	  on `<tip>`, and the working tree reverts to pre-close-out
474	  content, which looks alarming and isn't. `jj new` puts `@`
475	  back on top of the merge so the tree is right and the next
476	  commit continues from there. Skipping it doesn't break the
477	  publish; it leaves you working from the wrong parent.
478	- **Trailers survive.** The reshape changes `<closeout>`'s
479	  SHA but not its change ID, so the `ochid:` trailers stamped
480	  in step 1 stay valid in both directions. This is why the
481	  reshape is safe after the trailers are written.
482	- **Step 4 moves the bookmark sideways.** Step 1's SHA
483	  becomes unreachable; anyone who fetched between the two
484	  pushes holds a dangling commit. Consequently a
485	  [Commits backfill](#commits-backfill) must never read a
486	  SHA from that window; wait until step 4 lands.
487	- **Immutability.** No flag is needed on a long-lived topic
488	  bookmark. Only when `<closeout>` is already on `trunk()`
489	  does the rebase need `--ignore-immutable`, and then the
490	  push force-updates the target.
491	- **The bot repo is left for afterwards.** Step 4 touches only
492	  the work repo, so `.claude` still holds every session write
493	  from the whole procedure. `vc-x1 squash-push` folds that
494	  tail into the bot commit, and its change id survives the
495	  squash, so the work-side `ochid:` keeps resolving.
496	
497	#### Recovery
498	
499	- **Nothing is published between steps 2 and 3**, so the local
500	  reshape is undoable with `jj undo` / `jj op restore`.
501	- **A collapsed or mis-parented merge** (step 2 verification
502	  fails): undo and redo step 2 with the corrected revisions.
503	  Do not push a shape you did not intend; after step 4 the
504	  remote boundary is crossed and recovery is forward-only.
505	- **Working copy left beside the merge** (step 3 skipped):
506	  `jj new <closeout>` after the fact. Nothing published is
507	  affected (the bookmark was never wrong), but any commit
508	  made in the meantime branches off `<tip>` and needs a
509	  rebase onto the merge.
510	- **A wrong bookmark position**, however it arose:
511	  `jj bookmark set <bookmark> -r <closeout>` before pushing.
512	  If step 4 already published it, the fix is a second
513	  sideways move, not a rewrite.
514	
515	### vc-x1 push wrapper
516	
517	`vc-x1 push <bookmark>` wraps per-push mechanics. See
518	`vc-x1 push --help` for current flags. `<bookmark>` names a
519	work-repo bookmark only; the bot repo is always pinned to
520	`main` (see [.claude cadence](#claude-cadence)).
521	
522	**Current limitation**: only fully supports the
523	[Keep separate](#shape-at-close-out-push) shape; other
524	shapes need manual jj steps. Planned improvements are
525	project state, tracked in the project's `TODO.md`;
526	this protocol describes only the stable mechanism.
527	
528	### .claude cadence
529	
530	**Cadence**: one push = one bot-repo commit, paired
531	with every work-repo commit in that push.
532	
533	The `.claude` working copy accumulates session data
534	across the cycle; its change ID stays stable across
535	snapshots, `jj describe`, and the squash-push fold, so
536	work-repo `ochid:` trailers resolve.
537	
538	`.claude` is a linear journal: all session work lives
539	on `main`, regardless of the work-repo bookmark. **Do
540	not create or maintain bot-repo bookmarks that mirror
541	work-repo branches**, which risks the bot steering session
542	pushes to the wrong remote ref.
543	
544	Ending a session: if the user runs `/exit` there will be
545	session information created, which we don't worry about.
546	The user can close the terminal instead and `@` will
547	remain empty.
548	
549	### Bot communication at the reviews
550	
551	Use plain prose, no insider jargon ("Gate N signal",
552	"Checkpoint N", etc.):
553	
554	- **At Work review**, summarize what changed and stop.
555	  "Work complete. Please review."
556	- **At Commit Description review**, present `$TITLE`
557	  and `$BODY` explicitly; ask permission to commit/push.
558	  Don't spell out the full `vc-x1 push ... --title ...
559	  --body ...` invocation by default.
560	- **At Post close-out review**, surface the shape
561	  options (squash / merge / keep) and the push target;
562	  wait for the user's choice before any `jj squash` /
563	  `jj rebase` / `jj git push` invocation.
564	
565	### After push or squash-push: stop and wait
566	
567	After a **push** (crossing the remote boundary, by hand or
568	via the `vc-x1 push` wrapper, whose last stage publishes
569	the bot repo too) or a manual **squash-push** on the bot
570	repo, stop for the turn: no next step, edit, tool call, or
571	text output until the user directs otherwise. **Even when
572	the next step seems obvious, wait.**
573	
574	- **Scope**: the stop follows the user's directive, not the
575	  push. A standing directive covering more work ("finish
576	  the remaining ladder commits on your own") makes an
577	  intermediate push just a step; the hard stop lands on the
578	  turn's *final* push.
579	- **Why**: the bot repo is a live journal, so everything after
580	  the invocation (its own record, closing words) lands in
581	  `@` as a trailing tail. Between delegated pushes the tail
582	  rides into the next cycle's bot commit; the final push's
583	  tail has no next commit, and the bot's own squash-push is
584	  itself session data (`@` refills immediately), so only the
585	  user, after the turn, can capture it
586	  (`vc-x1 squash-push -R .claude`).
587	- **Silence**: put all closing words *before* the final
588	  push. The harness rejects an empty turn, so it may force a
589	  visible token after the tool returns; if so, emit a bare
590	  acknowledgment only (e.g. "landed"), never a summary,
591	  verification, or next-step offer. There is no "harmless"
592	  closing line after the push; that is a known slip.
593	- **Flush**: when the user wants `@` empty (no tail), they
594	  run `vc-x1 squash-push -R .claude` after the bot goes
595	  quiet, which flushes all bot session information into the
596	  published commit. Repeat if new writes land (see
597	  [Recovery](#recovery)).
598	
599	### Recovery
600	
601	- **If push exits before its last stage** (`push-work`
602	  succeeded but the bot-repo publish (`squash-push-bot`)
603	  didn't run), run the squash+push by hand:
604	
605	  ```
606	  vc-x1 squash-push -R .claude
607	  ```
608	
609	  It runs in-process, so a failure is a visible non-zero
610	  exit, with no log file to chase.
611	- **Run squash-push again if `@` is non-empty** after a
612	  pass (also desirable after extra activity by the bot's
613	  agents).
614	  - Why: the bot keeps writing session data while the
615	    command runs, so the invocation's own record plus any
616	    closing response land after the squash.
617	  - Safe to repeat: bot session data is append-only, so a
618	    re-run never conflicts or overwrites. (This could
619	    change; it is not under the user's control.)
620	  - No guarantees: events outside the bot's control can leave
621	    `@` non-empty; e.g. the bot's back end may decide to
622	    squash/consolidate session data, which can take minutes
623	    and land after the pass. The remedy is the same: just
624	    run squash-push again. This is why a single pass is never
625	    guaranteed to leave `@` empty.
626	- **Nothing to clear after an out-of-band recovery.** Push
627	  keeps no saved state, so whatever you do to the repos by
628	  hand is simply the state the next run sees.
629	- **Late work-repo tweak after the work-repo push succeeded**
630	  (e.g. updating AGENTS.md or memory) requires `jj
631	  squash --ignore-immutable` and a re-push; that is a
632	  remote rewrite and needs explicit approval like any
633	  push.
634	
635	## Iterative work
636	
637	When work for a single commit (the **target**) benefits
638	from incremental review, loop:
639	
640	1. `jj new -R .`: fresh empty `@` on top of the target.
641	2. Make the next round of changes.
642	3. User reviews the round (see
643	   [Reviewing changes](#reviewing-changes)).
644	4. `jj squash -R .` folds into the target and creates a
645	   new empty `@`.
646	5. If not done, go to step 2.
647	
648	Same jj mechanics as a
649	[sub-cycle ladder](#sub-cycle-ladders), but at
650	single-commit scope, so the version doesn't change.
651	
652	## Sub-cycle ladders
653	
654	When a Work commit subdivides into a sub-cycle (see
655	[Numbering](#numbering) for suffix nesting), its Work
656	commits will live as a local jj `@` chain and
657	**collapse into the sub-cycle's Close-out** before the
658	parent cycle continues. Ladder commits are scratch, for
659	review and bisection only.
660	
661	### Per-Work-commit contract within a ladder
662	
663	For each Work commit in the ladder:
664	
665	1. `jj new -R .`: create a fresh empty `@`.
666	2. Do the commit's work.
667	3. Run the fast validation (Rust example: `cargo test
668	   --bins`). **Non-negotiable**, because for code, build and
669	   clippy alone miss regressions until a later commit runs the
670	   full suite, raising bisection cost.
671	4. `jj describe -m "..." -m "..." -R .`: working title
672	   only; the sub-cycle Close-out collects everything
673	   into one final commit.
674	
675	**Nothing here is pushed.** The ladder is local until the
676	[Close-out squash](#close-out-squash-the-ladder), so no ladder
677	commit ever carries an `ochid:` trailer: the trailer is stamped
678	once, by `vc-x1 push`, on the squashed commit. Step 4 is
679	therefore first-time authoring of a scratch description, not a
680	rewrite of a published or stamped one, and is the named
681	exception to
682	[Re-describing](jj.md#re-describing-coordinate-first-and-keep-the-trailer).
683	
684	### Navigating the ladder
685	
686	Common moves:
687	
688	- `jj log -r '<base>::' -R .`: see the whole ladder
689	  from its base.
690	- `jj edit -r <prefix> -R .`: jump `@` to any ladder
691	  commit by chid prefix; useful for bisection.
692	- `jj edit @-- -R .`: quick-jump back two commits.
693	- `jj diff -r <chid> -R .`: review one commit in
694	  isolation.
695	
696	Modifications to any ladder commit rewrite it in place;
697	descendants auto-rebase.
698	
699	### Close-out: squash the ladder
700	
701	When all ladder Work commits are done and tests pass:
702	
703	```
704	jj squash --from "<base>..@-" --into @ -u -R .
705	```
706	
707	`<base>` is the parent of the first ladder commit; `-u`
708	keeps `@`'s description and discards the sources'.
709	After squash, history is linear: `<base> -> @`;
710	intermediate commits are auto-abandoned.
711	
712	Then `vc-x1 push <bookmark>` as for any other commit. This is
713	the ladder's first and only publish, and where its `ochid:`
714	trailer is stamped. The scratch descriptions written at step 4
715	of the
716	[per-Work-commit contract](#per-work-commit-contract-within-a-ladder)
717	never left the machine and never carried one, which is why
718	describing them freely is safe.
719	
720	For N = 1 the squash is a no-op (`<base>..@-` is empty
721	when `@-` is `<base>`); push the single commit directly.
722	
723	### Recovery
724	
725	If a ladder commit goes wrong, back out without losing
726	prior commits:
727	
728	- **Discard the current commit.** `jj abandon @ -R .`
729	  drops it; you get a fresh empty `@` on the same
730	  parent.
731	- **Edit an earlier commit.** `jj edit -r <chid> -R .`,
732	  make corrections, then `jj edit -r <last-ladder-chid>`
733	  to return. Descendants auto-rebase.
734	- **Discard the entire ladder.** `jj op log -R .` shows
735	  the op history; `jj op restore <op-id> -R .` reverts
736	  to that point. Full undo: removes *all* ladder work
737	  after the chosen op. Use only to start over.
738	
739	# References
740	
741	- [`jj.md > Revsets`](jj.md#revsets): revset primitives
742	  (chid/cid, `@`/`@-`/`@+`, `..`/`::` ranges, prefix matching).
743	- The per-commit `cargo test --bins` gate exists because a
744	  regression introduced in an early ladder commit can go
745	  uncaught until a later commit runs the full suite, raising
746	  bisection cost.
747

# Cycle protocol

This protocol uses [Prose form](prose.md#prose-form). It
contains instructions on how a commit cycle is accomplished.

Universal file, pinned to the template repository; do not edit
here. Project overrides go in [custom.md](../custom.md).

The artifact a cycle produces is whatever the bot generates from
the conversation: code, prose, an image, a song, a screenplay.
The steps below use a Rust crate as the running example (the
cargo cycle, `Cargo.toml` versioning); substitute your medium's
equivalents. This project's manifest is recorded in
[versioning.md](versioning.md).

## Cycles

A cycle has three phases:

- **[Preparation](#preparation)** (`X.Y.Z-0`): the cycle's
  first commit, when it needs setup (a lightweight cycle omits
  it and starts at `-1`; see
  [versioning.md](versioning.md#step-numbering)). Sets up the
  cycle:
  - Bump the version-of-record to `X.Y.Z-0` (where it lives
    and the suffix scheme are project-specific; see
    [versioning.md](versioning.md)).
  - Pick up a `## Todo` item (typically the top-ranked,
    #1) into `## In Progress` (bold title + succinct problem
    statement + plan ladder).
  - Open the [chores section](#chores-sections).
- **[Work-N](#work-n)** (`X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...): the
  commits that implement the change. As many as the change
  needs; each runs through the
  [per-commit flow](#per-commit-flow).
- **[Close-out](#close-out)** (bare `X.Y.Z`): the cycle's
  last commit. Bookkeeping only:
  - Move the picked-up item to a one-line entry in
    `## Done`.
  - Move the `## In Progress` block into the
    [chores section](#chores-sections).
  - Optionally update `notes/README.md` if functionality
    changed.

A cycle's commits are published to the project remote
either incrementally or as one batch at close-out; the
result must always be published at close-out. See
[Pushing](#pushing).

**Sub-cycles.** When a Work commit's scope grows enough to
warrant its own ladder, it subdivides: `X.Y.Z-3.0`
Preparation, `X.Y.Z-3.1` / `X.Y.Z-3.2` Work, `X.Y.Z-3`
Close-out. The same three-phase shape applies recursively
at every depth. See [Numbering](#numbering) for the
suffix rule and [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders)
for the local-ladder mechanics.

## Chores sections

A **chores section** is a `##` section in `notes/chores/chores-NN.md` recording landed work.
In general, every commit that lands on the permanent branch should have a rung in some
section's as-built ladder in a chores file.

The phrase **"Open" the chores section** means append a `##` header to the current
`notes/chores/chores-NN.md` with the title it records (e.g. `## refactor: foo bar`), add the
file's `## Table of Contents` entry, and start the **as-built ladder**: one
`- [[N]] X.Y.Z[-n] <title>` rung per commit the section records, each opening with the literal
`[[N]]` placeholder. **Each work commit then appends its own rung + narrative note as it
lands**, so the chores record is built up per commit, not held back and written all at once at
close-out; close-out only *finalizes* (title sync, design subsections, retiring the
`## In Progress` block). Rung placeholders are backfilled later, once their commits are
permanent (see [Commits backfill](#commits-backfill) below).

Fuller chores conventions (content rules, header sync, design subsection pattern, ladder and
reference formatting, the Table of Contents) live in
[Chores conventions](notes.md#chores-conventions).

### Commits backfill

An as-built ladder rung cites its commit by SHA, but a SHA isn't stable until the commit lands
on a **permanent branch** (`main`, or a long-lived release/patch branch that won't be
rewritten); a rebase or squash rewrites it on the way. So:

- A rung is **written with the literal `[[N]]` placeholder**.
- **Backfill once the commit is on a permanent branch**, where its SHA is final. A commit
  can't record its own SHA (that would change the hash), so the fill always lands one push
  later: **each push backfills the rungs of the commits the previous push made permanent.** On
  a topic branch the sections instead wait until the branch lands, so no SHA is ever written
  that a later rebase could invalidate.
- A deliberate rewrite of already-recorded commits (a coordinated re-describe, a retroactive
  reshape) invalidates their recorded SHAs. Re-record them once the rewrite is published, on
  the same one-push-later timing.

Each rung carries its own `[N]` ref, with the commit URL + 40-hex SHA in the file's
`# References` (format in
[Chores commit references](notes.md#chores-commit-references)). A section's `##`
title matches its close-out commit title, and each rung's text its own commit title, so a rare
deliberate rewrite of a permanent-branch commit re-syncs via `git log --grep "<title>"`.
Sections that predate the ladder form keep their grandfathered `Commits:` lines.

The per-push cadence is a project choice, not dogma. A **per-close-out** model (recording a
cycle's SHAs at its close-out) is equally valid. The one invariant: a recorded SHA must be
permanent.

## Preparation

The cycle's first commit (`X.Y.Z-0`), when the cycle needs
setup (a lightweight cycle omits it; see
[versioning.md](versioning.md#step-numbering)):

- **Bump the version-of-record** to `X.Y.Z-0`. Where it
  lives, the suffix scheme, and any derived files (a
  lockfile, a sourced manifest version) are
  project-specific; see [versioning.md](versioning.md).
- **Move a `## Todo` item** (if the cycle has one) into
  `## In Progress` and the todo item should have:
  - A **bold title line**, which will be the chores
    section header, minus the `## ` prefix.
  - A **succinct problem statement**; add if one is needed
  - A **plan ladder**.
- **Open the [chores section](#chores-sections)**: append a
  `##` header with the title it records, the cycle's
  anticipated close-out title.

## Work-N

The cycle's work commits (`X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...)
implement the change. As many as needed:

- Each commit runs through the
  **[per-commit flow](#per-commit-flow)**.
- **Interim pushes** are optional (backup, progress
  visibility).
- Close-out is the only mandatory push (see
  [Pushing](#pushing)).
- **Subdivide into a sub-cycle** if a Work commit's
  scope grows enough (see
  [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders)).

## Close-out

The cycle's last commit (bare `X.Y.Z`) does bookkeeping
only, and the commit body describes that bookkeeping, not
what happens post-squash:

- **Move the picked-up item** from `## In Progress` to a
  one-line entry (with a chores `[N]` ref) in `## Done`.
- **Finalize the chores section** (opened during Preparation
  and grown per commit; see [Chores sections](#chores-sections)):
  - The problem statement is already the chores intro (written
    when the section was opened) and the plan ladder is already
    the `### As-built ladder` (a rung appended per commit), so
    close-out only *finalizes*, it does not cut-and-paste.
  - Sync the chores header to the **final** commit title if the
    cycle's scope shifted; update every anchor back-reference.
  - Add any `### design subsections`; optional `### Outcome`
    notes.
  - Replace the `## In Progress` cycle block with
    `_No cycle currently in progress._`. Under a multi-cycle
    program (program `###`, current stage `####`) this retires
    the stage `####` only; the program heading and its ladder
    stay, the shipped rung flipped `(done)`, so the marker
    sits inside the program block until the next stage is
    picked up.
- **Update `notes/README.md`** if functionality changed
  (new flags, new subcommands, changed behavior).

Whether to **squash** the cycle into one commit before the
publishing push, or push as-is, is decided at push time; see
[Pushing](#pushing).

## Numbering

Each commit's phase is encoded in the version suffix: `-0`
Preparation, `-1`/`-2`/... Work, bare `X.Y.Z` Close-out,
recursively for sub-cycles. The full scheme (disambiguation,
nesting, optional Preparation, the project's version-of-record
format, and the per-phase bump) lives in
[versioning.md](versioning.md#step-numbering), which is the
single source of truth for this repo's versioning.

## Per-commit flow

Every commit (Preparation, each Work commit, Close-out) goes
through:

1. **Mark this commit `(current)`** as the first edit in
   `TODO.md > ## In Progress` (`TODO.md` is at the repo
   root).
2. **Do the work** (see [Iterative work](#iterative-work)
   for the loop-and-squash technique).
3. **Flip this commit `(current)` -> `(done)`** in `## In
   Progress`, before the cargo cycle and the commit.
4. **Validate the artifact**, a medium-specific step, skip-able
   for notes-only commits, mandatory at close-out. For the Rust
   example the cargo cycle is:
   1. `cargo fmt`
   2. `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`
   3. `cargo test`
   4. `cargo install --path . --locked`
   5. (re-test if anything substantive changed)
5. **Work review.** Stop *before* writing any description;
   tell the user "ready to commit." The user reviews the
   changes and we iterate until complete.
6. **Write the commit description**; see
   [Commit description](#commit-description).
7. **Commit Description review.** Show the title + body
   and stop. The user reviews the description. Iterate.
8. **Commit + push.** Hand the approved title/body to
   `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "..." --body "..."`, whose
   commit stages commit both repos and stamp the `ochid:`
   trailers. Never pre-commit the rung with `jj commit`: an
   empty `@` at push mints a stamped empty duplicate
   (bugs.md #6). Push approval is per-push, so step 7's
   review covers it only when the user's go explicitly
   includes the push.

**Two overrides apply:**

- **Deviation or question.** Any time the work deviates
  from the agreed plan, or a question arises, stop and
  surface it; don't push through.
- **ESC-ESC.** The user can interrupt at any point to pull
  a review or question forward.

## Commit description

[Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/):

```
<type>: <short description>
<type>(scope): <short description>   # optional scope
```

Titles carry **no trailing `(<version>)` suffix**. The
version-of-record (where it lives and its bump cadence, see
[versioning.md](versioning.md)) is useful for confirming
you're running the version you're testing, not a per-commit
title marker. We think per-commit version-in-title is
unstable on large projects: many changes are in flight
simultaneously, and a version is only stable once merged into
the main repo, so titles don't carry one.

### Title

- <=72 chars total.
- Common types: `feat`, `fix`, `refactor`, `test`,
  `docs`, `chore`; optional `(scope)` in parentheses after
  the type, per the spec.
- Favor terse phrasings.
- **Distinct per step.** Each of a cycle's commits gets its
  own descriptive title (no shared cycle title with a step
  marker). Share a greppable stem across the cycle's titles
  (e.g. `ring buffer`) so `git log --grep` collects them; the
  chores section header matches the close-out title. See
  [Conventional-commit shape](prose.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit).

### Body

[Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) (intro + bullets),
wrap ≤72. Bullet content differs per repo:

- **Work-repo body**: file-by-file. One bullet per file
  changed (file plus a one-line gist), in short sentence
  fragments (full sentences are discouraged). Sub-bullets
  for files with multiple distinct changes:

  ```
  - path/to/file1
    - first distinct change
    - second distinct change, wrapping to next line
       with continuation indented 5
  ```

  The list **opens with the version bump** as its first
  bullet, for the Rust example
  `- Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock: vX.Y.Z-xxxx` (generally:
  the medium's version-of-record files); `-xxxx` stands for
  the whole suffix, nested or not (`v0.78.0-1`,
  `v0.78.0-3.1`), per
  [versioning.md](versioning.md#grammar-and-storage). Titles stay
  version-free (above), so this first bullet is the
  version's durable, visible home, and log viewers (e.g.
  gitk's message pane) show it without opening the commit's
  file list. Adopted 2026-07-24.

  The file-by-file list is the source of truth for the
  cycle's mechanical change record. Chores carries the
  narrative + design, not a copy of it. Promote any
  "why" beyond one sentence to a chores `###` subsection.

- **Bot-repo (`.claude`) body**: bullets describe
  in-session activity rather than work-repo changes.

### Trailer

`ochid:` as the last line of the body; see
[Cross-repo linking (ochid trailers)](jj.md#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)
in agent-data/jj.md for the convention.

For breaking changes, use the hyphenated `BREAKING-CHANGE:`
trailer key. `BREAKING CHANGE:` (with a space) is the only
space-separated key the Conventional Commits spec allows; the
hyphenated form is also valid and avoids the space ambiguity.

## Reviewing changes

Work review looks at the **uncommitted working-copy diff**,
on the way to commit. The user opens diffs in their
editor (Zed, VSCode); jj commands are for terminal:

- `jj diff`: working-copy diff (uncommitted)
- `jj diff -r @-`: diff of the previous commit
- `jj diff --from <X> --to <Y>`: any two revisions
- `jj show -r <X>`: description + diff for one rev

Don't `jj edit -r @-` to view a past commit, because that marks
it mutable and shifts `@`; use `jj diff -r @-` or
`jj show -r @-`.

No preflight while a review iterates: `fmt` / `clippy` / `test`
wait until the review settles, since `fmt` mutates files in ways
that interact badly with the user's mid-review edits. Validation
runs once, on the settled state, per the per-commit checklist.

See [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders) for the
close-out squash recipe and recovery; revset primitives
are in [`jj.md > Revsets`](jj.md#revsets).

## Pushing

### Policy

Push is **discretionary** during the cycle (backup,
progress visibility) and **mandatory at close-out**, since
the cycle's result must be published.

**Approval is per-push.** Every push (any repo, any kind:
cycle push, interim backup, recovery/surgery force-push)
happens only after the user has reviewed the changes to be
published and explicitly approved that specific push.
Approval of a plan that *includes* a push does not authorize
the push itself; stop and ask again at the moment of pushing.

**Default is interactive; an explicit scoped delegation waives
the gates.** The gates above (per-push approval, the
commit-description review that shows title+body and stops, and
the hard stop after push/squash-push) are the *interactive
default*.
They yield when the user **explicitly** delegates a complete,
bounded task and authorizes carrying it through ("do all of X
and push each step, don't check in"). The bot then proceeds
through that task's commits and pushes without stopping, and
continues past each push to the next step. Conditions:

- **Explicit grant.** Never inferred from a task merely being
  well-scoped; the user's words must authorize unattended
  completion. "Commit and push" (or "then push") names the
  destination, not a waiver: it authorizes the push *after*
  the normal work review and description review, not skipping
  them. Only wording that explicitly waives the stops ("don't
  check in", "no need to review", "carry it through
  unattended") waives them.
- **Bounded goal.** Covers the named task only; does not carry
  to the next task or a vaguer follow-on.
- **Destructive ops still pause.** Delegation covers the task's
  ordinary commits and pushes; it does *not* pre-authorize a
  genuinely irreversible action (force-push over published
  history, history rewrite, deleting a remote branch). Those can
  permanently destroy work and aren't a normal cycle step, so the
  bot flags one before acting. An ordinary delegated cycle never
  reaches this.
- **Still transparent.** Report each commit/push as it lands
  (title + outcome) so the user can catch up.
- **When in doubt, ask.** Ambiguous authorization falls back to
  per-push approval.

### Shape at close-out push

At close-out the cycle's *work* is done; its *published
shape* is the remaining choice, made at push time. Surface
the options and get user approval before pushing. Once on
the target, changing shape is a remote rewrite (force-push,
needs approval), so choose deliberately.

- **Squash to one commit**: single entry on the target.
  Right for straightforward changes where the Work-N is
  focused on one or two files.
- **Trapezoid** (a `git merge --no-ff` merge commit)
  *(current default)*: the target gains a merge commit
  (`X.Y.Z`) whose first parent is the trunk line and whose
  second parent is the cycle's ladder, so
  `git log --first-parent` reads one commit per cycle while
  every rung stays reachable. See
  [Trapezoid close-out recipe](#trapezoid-close-out-recipe)
  for the full sequence.
- **Keep separate**: one commit per cycle entry on
  `main`. Use when the decomposition itself is
  informative. Each chores section keeps its own header /
  ladder refs; no consolidation churn.

A squash is set up before invoking `vc-x1 push`; a trapezoid
is reshaped between two pushes (the recipe below). For any
other shape, drive `jj git push` directly.

### Trapezoid close-out recipe

A [trapezoid](#shape-at-close-out-push) close-out is
published in four steps: an ordinary close-out push, a
two-command reshape, and a second push that re-points the
bookmark at the reshaped commit.

```
  main line   ...──<base>──────────────────<closeout>──
                      \                    /
  ladder             <rung-1>──...──<tip>─┘
```

- `<base>`: the **parent of the ladder's first rung**, which
  is the trunk position when the cycle opened. It becomes the
  first parent.
- `<tip>`: the cycle's last Work commit. It becomes the
  second parent.
- `<closeout>`: the close-out commit, created by step 1.

The steps. Only step 1 is a `vc-x1 push`; the rest is jj,
because after step 1 the commits already exist and all that
remains is reshaping and publishing them:

1. `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "..." --body "..."`
   - the ordinary close-out push. It commits both repos, stamps the
   `ochid:` trailers, and publishes `<closeout>` linearly.
2. `jj rebase -r <closeout> --onto <base> --onto <tip>`
   - `<closeout>` becomes the merge. Parent order is the
   argument order.
3. `jj new <closeout>`
   -  puts an empty `@` above the merge.
4. `jj git push --bookmark <bookmark> -R .`
   - publishes the reshaped commit. The bookmark needs no `jj bookmark set`:
   it follows the rewrite in step 2 automatically. The bot
   repo is untouched, and its session tail goes out with a
   separate `vc-x1 squash-push` afterwards.

**Step 4 is not a `vc-x1 push`** (corrected at the `0.77.0`
close-out, which tried it). Push runs its whole pipeline or
none of it, and the bot repo is never quiet for long: by the
time the reshape is done, `.claude` holds the session writes
from steps 1-3, so `commit-bot` wants to run and the message
stage demands a title for it. The result is a bot-side
requirement blocking a work-side publish that needs nothing
but a moved ref. Publishing an already-made commit is a
different operation from committing and publishing, and only
the latter is push's job.

#### Details

- **Verify two parents before step 4.** `jj log -r <closeout>
  -T 'parents.map(|p| p.change_id().short(8))'` must list
  both. jj preserves the second parent even though `<base>`
  is an ancestor of `<tip>` (observed at `0.74.0`, `0.75.0`,
  `0.76.0`), but a collapsed merge is indistinguishable from
  a correct one in `jj log --no-graph` and is only visible
  once published.
- **`<base>` is not always the previous close-out.** A docs
  or planning interlude between cycles sits on the trunk line
  and must stay there; take the parent of the ladder's first
  rung, not the last close-out.
- **Step 3 is about `@`, not the bookmark.** The bookmark
  follows the rewrite in step 2 on its own. What step 2
  leaves misplaced is the working copy: `jj rebase -r`
  re-parents descendants onto the rebased commit's **old**
  parent, so the empty `@` from step 1 lands beside the merge
  on `<tip>`, and the working tree reverts to pre-close-out
  content, which looks alarming and isn't. `jj new` puts `@`
  back on top of the merge so the tree is right and the next
  commit continues from there. Skipping it doesn't break the
  publish; it leaves you working from the wrong parent.
- **Trailers survive.** The reshape changes `<closeout>`'s
  SHA but not its change ID, so the `ochid:` trailers stamped
  in step 1 stay valid in both directions. This is why the
  reshape is safe after the trailers are written.
- **Step 4 moves the bookmark sideways.** Step 1's SHA
  becomes unreachable; anyone who fetched between the two
  pushes holds a dangling commit. Consequently a
  [Commits backfill](#commits-backfill) must never read a
  SHA from that window; wait until step 4 lands.
- **Immutability.** No flag is needed on a long-lived topic
  bookmark. Only when `<closeout>` is already on `trunk()`
  does the rebase need `--ignore-immutable`, and then the
  push force-updates the target.
- **The bot repo is left for afterwards.** Step 4 touches only
  the work repo, so `.claude` still holds every session write
  from the whole procedure. `vc-x1 squash-push` folds that
  tail into the bot commit, and its change id survives the
  squash, so the work-side `ochid:` keeps resolving.

#### Recovery

- **Nothing is published between steps 2 and 3**, so the local
  reshape is undoable with `jj undo` / `jj op restore`.
- **A collapsed or mis-parented merge** (step 2 verification
  fails): undo and redo step 2 with the corrected revisions.
  Do not push a shape you did not intend; after step 4 the
  remote boundary is crossed and recovery is forward-only.
- **Working copy left beside the merge** (step 3 skipped):
  `jj new <closeout>` after the fact. Nothing published is
  affected (the bookmark was never wrong), but any commit
  made in the meantime branches off `<tip>` and needs a
  rebase onto the merge.
- **A wrong bookmark position**, however it arose:
  `jj bookmark set <bookmark> -r <closeout>` before pushing.
  If step 4 already published it, the fix is a second
  sideways move, not a rewrite.

### vc-x1 push wrapper

`vc-x1 push <bookmark>` wraps per-push mechanics. See
`vc-x1 push --help` for current flags. `<bookmark>` names a
work-repo bookmark only; the bot repo is always pinned to
`main` (see [.claude cadence](#claude-cadence)).

**Current limitation**: only fully supports the
[Keep separate](#shape-at-close-out-push) shape; other
shapes need manual jj steps. Planned improvements are
project state, tracked in the project's `TODO.md`;
this protocol describes only the stable mechanism.

### .claude cadence

**Cadence**: one push = one bot-repo commit, paired
with every work-repo commit in that push.

The `.claude` working copy accumulates session data
across the cycle; its change ID stays stable across
snapshots, `jj describe`, and the squash-push fold, so
work-repo `ochid:` trailers resolve.

`.claude` is a linear journal: all session work lives
on `main`, regardless of the work-repo bookmark. **Do
not create or maintain bot-repo bookmarks that mirror
work-repo branches**, which risks the bot steering session
pushes to the wrong remote ref.

Ending a session: if the user runs `/exit` there will be
session information created, which we don't worry about.
The user can close the terminal instead and `@` will
remain empty.

### Bot communication at the reviews

Use plain prose, no insider jargon ("Gate N signal",
"Checkpoint N", etc.):

- **At Work review**, summarize what changed and stop.
  "Work complete. Please review."
- **At Commit Description review**, present `$TITLE`
  and `$BODY` explicitly; ask permission to commit/push.
  Don't spell out the full `vc-x1 push ... --title ...
  --body ...` invocation by default.
- **At Post close-out review**, surface the shape
  options (squash / merge / keep) and the push target;
  wait for the user's choice before any `jj squash` /
  `jj rebase` / `jj git push` invocation.

### After push or squash-push: stop and wait

After a **push** (crossing the remote boundary, by hand or
via the `vc-x1 push` wrapper, whose last stage publishes
the bot repo too) or a manual **squash-push** on the bot
repo, stop for the turn: no next step, edit, tool call, or
text output until the user directs otherwise. **Even when
the next step seems obvious, wait.**

- **Scope**: the stop follows the user's directive, not the
  push. A standing directive covering more work ("finish
  the remaining ladder commits on your own") makes an
  intermediate push just a step; the hard stop lands on the
  turn's *final* push.
- **Why**: the bot repo is a live journal, so everything after
  the invocation (its own record, closing words) lands in
  `@` as a trailing tail. Between delegated pushes the tail
  rides into the next cycle's bot commit; the final push's
  tail has no next commit, and the bot's own squash-push is
  itself session data (`@` refills immediately), so only the
  user, after the turn, can capture it
  (`vc-x1 squash-push -R .claude`).
- **Silence**: put all closing words *before* the final
  push. The harness rejects an empty turn, so it may force a
  visible token after the tool returns; if so, emit a bare
  acknowledgment only (e.g. "landed"), never a summary,
  verification, or next-step offer. There is no "harmless"
  closing line after the push; that is a known slip.
- **Flush**: when the user wants `@` empty (no tail), they
  run `vc-x1 squash-push -R .claude` after the bot goes
  quiet, which flushes all bot session information into the
  published commit. Repeat if new writes land (see
  [Recovery](#recovery)).

### Recovery

- **If push exits before its last stage** (`push-work`
  succeeded but the bot-repo publish (`squash-push-bot`)
  didn't run), run the squash+push by hand:

  ```
  vc-x1 squash-push -R .claude
  ```

  It runs in-process, so a failure is a visible non-zero
  exit, with no log file to chase.
- **Run squash-push again if `@` is non-empty** after a
  pass (also desirable after extra activity by the bot's
  agents).
  - Why: the bot keeps writing session data while the
    command runs, so the invocation's own record plus any
    closing response land after the squash.
  - Safe to repeat: bot session data is append-only, so a
    re-run never conflicts or overwrites. (This could
    change; it is not under the user's control.)
  - No guarantees: events outside the bot's control can leave
    `@` non-empty; e.g. the bot's back end may decide to
    squash/consolidate session data, which can take minutes
    and land after the pass. The remedy is the same: just
    run squash-push again. This is why a single pass is never
    guaranteed to leave `@` empty.
- **Nothing to clear after an out-of-band recovery.** Push
  keeps no saved state, so whatever you do to the repos by
  hand is simply the state the next run sees.
- **Late work-repo tweak after the work-repo push succeeded**
  (e.g. updating AGENTS.md or memory) requires `jj
  squash --ignore-immutable` and a re-push; that is a
  remote rewrite and needs explicit approval like any
  push.

## Iterative work

When work for a single commit (the **target**) benefits
from incremental review, loop:

1. `jj new -R .`: fresh empty `@` on top of the target.
2. Make the next round of changes.
3. User reviews the round (see
   [Reviewing changes](#reviewing-changes)).
4. `jj squash -R .` folds into the target and creates a
   new empty `@`.
5. If not done, go to step 2.

Same jj mechanics as a
[sub-cycle ladder](#sub-cycle-ladders), but at
single-commit scope, so the version doesn't change.

## Sub-cycle ladders

When a Work commit subdivides into a sub-cycle (see
[Numbering](#numbering) for suffix nesting), its Work
commits will live as a local jj `@` chain and
**collapse into the sub-cycle's Close-out** before the
parent cycle continues. Ladder commits are scratch, for
review and bisection only.

### Per-Work-commit contract within a ladder

For each Work commit in the ladder:

1. `jj new -R .`: create a fresh empty `@`.
2. Do the commit's work.
3. Run the fast validation (Rust example: `cargo test
   --bins`). **Non-negotiable**, because for code, build and
   clippy alone miss regressions until a later commit runs the
   full suite, raising bisection cost.
4. `jj describe -m "..." -m "..." -R .`: working title
   only; the sub-cycle Close-out collects everything
   into one final commit.

**Nothing here is pushed.** The ladder is local until the
[Close-out squash](#close-out-squash-the-ladder), so no ladder
commit ever carries an `ochid:` trailer: the trailer is stamped
once, by `vc-x1 push`, on the squashed commit. Step 4 is
therefore first-time authoring of a scratch description, not a
rewrite of a published or stamped one, and is the named
exception to
[Re-describing](jj.md#re-describing-coordinate-first-and-keep-the-trailer).

### Navigating the ladder

Common moves:

- `jj log -r '<base>::' -R .`: see the whole ladder
  from its base.
- `jj edit -r <prefix> -R .`: jump `@` to any ladder
  commit by chid prefix; useful for bisection.
- `jj edit @-- -R .`: quick-jump back two commits.
- `jj diff -r <chid> -R .`: review one commit in
  isolation.

Modifications to any ladder commit rewrite it in place;
descendants auto-rebase.

### Close-out: squash the ladder

When all ladder Work commits are done and tests pass:

```
jj squash --from "<base>..@-" --into @ -u -R .
```

`<base>` is the parent of the first ladder commit; `-u`
keeps `@`'s description and discards the sources'.
After squash, history is linear: `<base> -> @`;
intermediate commits are auto-abandoned.

Then `vc-x1 push <bookmark>` as for any other commit. This is
the ladder's first and only publish, and where its `ochid:`
trailer is stamped. The scratch descriptions written at step 4
of the
[per-Work-commit contract](#per-work-commit-contract-within-a-ladder)
never left the machine and never carried one, which is why
describing them freely is safe.

For N = 1 the squash is a no-op (`<base>..@-` is empty
when `@-` is `<base>`); push the single commit directly.

### Recovery

If a ladder commit goes wrong, back out without losing
prior commits:

- **Discard the current commit.** `jj abandon @ -R .`
  drops it; you get a fresh empty `@` on the same
  parent.
- **Edit an earlier commit.** `jj edit -r <chid> -R .`,
  make corrections, then `jj edit -r <last-ladder-chid>`
  to return. Descendants auto-rebase.
- **Discard the entire ladder.** `jj op log -R .` shows
  the op history; `jj op restore <op-id> -R .` reverts
  to that point. Full undo: removes *all* ladder work
  after the chosen op. Use only to start over.

# References

- [`jj.md > Revsets`](jj.md#revsets): revset primitives
  (chid/cid, `@`/`@-`/`@+`, `..`/`::` ranges, prefix matching).
- The per-commit `cargo test --bins` gate exists because a
  regression introduced in an early ladder commit can go
  uncaught until a later commit runs the full suite, raising
  bisection cost.
