1	# Cycle protocol
2	
3	This protocol uses [Prose form](../agent-data/prose.md#prose-form). It
4	contains instructions on how a commit cycle is accomplished.
5	
6	The artifact a cycle produces is whatever the bot generates from
7	the conversation: code, prose, an image, a song, a screenplay.
8	The steps below use a Rust crate as the running example (the
9	cargo cycle, `Cargo.toml` versioning); substitute your medium's
10	equivalents. This project's manifest is recorded in
11	[versioning.md](versioning.md).
12	
13	## Cycles
14	
15	A cycle has three phases:
16	
17	- **[Preparation](#preparation)**: the cycle's first commit, when it needs setup (a lightweight
18	  cycle omits it and starts at its first Work step). Sets up the cycle:
19	  - Bump the version-of-record (where it lives and the suffix scheme are project-specific; see
20	    [versioning.md](versioning.md)).
21	  - Pick up a `## Todo` item (typically the top-ranked, #1)
22	    into `## In Progress` as the cycle's
23	    [six provisional items](#preparation): title, problem
24	    statement, solution statement, acceptance check, ladder,
25	    deliberation.
26	  - Create the cycle's topic bookmark.
27	  - Nothing is opened in the chores file; the block is the
28	    cycle's only home until close-out moves it.
29	- **[Work-N](#work-n)**: the commits that implement the change. As many as the change needs;
30	  each runs through the [per-commit flow](#per-commit-flow).
31	- **[Close-out](#close-out)**: the cycle's last commit. Bookkeeping only:
32	  - Run the acceptance check and record what it showed.
33	  - Finalize the six items, then move the block into
34	    `notes/chores/`, which creates the
35	    [chores section](#chores-sections).
36	  - Write the `## Done` entry and clear `## In Progress`.
37	  - Land the cycle's bookmark.
38	  - Optionally update `notes/README.md` if functionality
39	    changed.
40	
41	A cycle's commits are published to the project remote
42	either incrementally or as one batch at close-out; the
43	result must always be published at close-out. See
44	[Pushing](#pushing).
45	
46	**Sub-cycles.** When a Work commit's scope grows enough to warrant its own ladder, it subdivides
47	into its own Preparation / Work / Close-out. The same three-phase shape applies recursively at
48	every depth, and a sub-ladder's rungs are titles like any other. See
49	[Step naming](#step-naming) for how a step is identified and
50	[Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders) for the local-ladder mechanics.
51	
52	## Chores sections
53	
54	A **chores section** is a `##` section in
55	`notes/chores/chores-NN.md` recording landed work. In
56	general, every commit that lands on the permanent branch
57	should have a reference to it on a rung of its section's
58	as-built ladder in a chores file.
59	
60	**A cycle's record has one home at a time.** While the cycle
61	runs it lives entirely in `TODO.md > ## In Progress`, as the
62	[six provisional items](#preparation) written at Preparation
63	and revised as steps land. At close-out the whole block
64	**moves** into the chores file, becoming that cycle's `##`
65	section. It is never written in two places, so there is
66	nothing to keep in sync and nothing to write twice.
67	
68	The move is mechanical, four transforms and no rewriting:
69	
70	- **Heading levels shift one deeper**: the block's `###`
71	  title becomes the section's `##`, and its `####` items
72	  become `###`. Anchors survive untouched, because GitHub
73	  slugs derive from the heading's *text*, not its level.
74	- **Rung refs renumber** into the destination file's `[N]`
75	  namespace (see [Reference numbering](../agent-data/notes.md#reference-numbering)).
76	- **Repo-root-relative links gain `../`**, since the block
77	  moves from the root into `notes/chores/`.
78	- **The block's own forward-looking notes are rewritten**,
79	  since they described a future that has now happened.
80	
81	Two of those fail *silently*: a mis-renumbered ref and an
82	un-rebased link render as plain text or a 404 rather than
83	erroring. Check both by hand until a `validate-repo` exists.
84	
85	A single-commit cycle's ladder is one rung, its close-out.
86	Rung placeholders are backfilled once the commit is
87	permanent (see [Commits backfill](#commits-backfill) below).
88	
89	The move also appends the section's title-only
90	`- [<title>](#<anchor>)` entry to the file's
91	`## Table of Contents`.
92	
93	Adopted from vc-x1, which trialled it through a full cycle
94	and kept it: the dual maintenance disappeared, and the
95	narrative did not thin out from being written in `TODO.md`,
96	which was the risk.
97	
98	Fuller chores conventions (content rules, header sync,
99	design subsection pattern, rung / reference formatting)
100	live in
101	[agent-data/notes.md](../agent-data/notes.md#chores-conventions).
102	
103	### Commits backfill
104	
105	An as-built ladder rung cites its commit by SHA and records the version that commit carried, and
106	neither is stable until the commit lands on a **permanent branch** (`main`, or a long-lived
107	release/patch branch that won't be rewritten); a rebase or squash rewrites the SHA and may
108	renumber the version on the way. So:
109	
110	- A rung is **written with the literal `[[N]]` placeholder and no version**.
111	- **Backfill once the commit is on a permanent branch**, where both are final. A commit can't
112	  record its own SHA (that would change the hash), so the fill always lands one push later:
113	  **each push backfills the rungs of the commits the previous push made permanent.** On a topic
114	  branch the sections instead wait until the branch lands, so nothing is ever written that a
115	  later rebase could invalidate.
116	
117	Backfill replaces the placeholder with a file-local `[[N]]` ref, defined as the commit URL +
118	40-hex SHA in the file's `# References` (format in agent-data/notes.md
119	[Chores commit references](../agent-data/notes.md#chores-commit-references)), and writes the
120	version ahead of the title. Sections predating the ladder form keep their legacy `Commits:`
121	lines; backfill those where they exist. A section's `##` title matches its commit title, so a
122	rare deliberate rewrite of a permanent-branch commit re-syncs via `git log --grep "<title>"`.
123	
124	The per-push cadence is a project choice, not dogma: a **per-close-out** model (recording a
125	cycle's SHAs at its close-out) is equally valid. The one invariant: what a rung records must be
126	permanent.
127	
128	## Preparation
129	
130	The cycle's first commit, when the cycle needs setup (a lightweight cycle omits it; see
131	[versioning.md](versioning.md#suffix-scheme)):
132	
133	- **Bump the version-of-record.** Where it lives, the suffix scheme, and any derived files (a
134	  lockfile, a sourced manifest version) are project-specific; see
135	  [versioning.md](versioning.md).
136	- **Move a `## Todo` item** (if the cycle has one) into
137	  `## In Progress`, and write the cycle's **six provisional
138	  items** there. All six are required, all six are revised
139	  as steps land, and all six move to chores at close-out.
140	  The first is a `###` heading; the rest are `####` headings
141	  under it:
142	  - the **title**, which becomes the chores section header.
143	  - the **problem statement**: what is wrong, in a sentence
144	    or two.
145	  - the **solution statement**: what will be done about it,
146	    broad. Provisional here, since it is written before the
147	    work; the close-out's commit body carries the final one.
148	  - the **acceptance check**: the measure of "are you
149	    finished?". Not the per-commit validation, which asks
150	    whether the artifact still works; this asks whether the
151	    thing the cycle promised actually happened, specifically
152	    enough that a reader can run it.
153	  - the **ladder**: one rung per step, a bare title plus a
154	    `(current)` / `(done)` marker.
155	  - the **deliberation**: how the five above were decided,
156	    alternatives weighed, costs accepted. `_None._` when
157	    there was nothing to deliberate, which is a real answer
158	    and different from having forgotten to write it.
159	
160	Nothing is opened in the chores file at Preparation. The
161	section is created at close-out by moving this block; see
162	[Chores sections](#chores-sections).
163	
164	**Why an acceptance check, and why it is provisional.** A
165	cycle's own per-commit checklists can all pass while its
166	banner claim is false: vc-x1's seven-cycle program opened
167	against "end subprocess spawning" and its close-out claimed
168	the goal met, with about twenty spawn sites surviving, two
169	inside the facade the program built. Being provisional, the
170	check can also be revised *toward* what was achieved, which
171	is the same failure by a slower route. So a changed check is
172	one of the things the deliberation exists to justify.
173	
174	## Work-N
175	
176	The cycle's work commits implement the change. As many as needed:
177	
178	- Each commit runs through the
179	  **[per-commit flow](#per-commit-flow)**.
180	- **Interim pushes** are optional (backup, progress
181	  visibility).
182	- Close-out is the only mandatory push (see
183	  [Pushing](#pushing)).
184	- **Subdivide into a sub-cycle** if a Work commit's
185	  scope grows enough (see
186	  [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders)).
187	
188	## Close-out
189	
190	The cycle's last commit does bookkeeping only, and the commit body describes that bookkeeping,
191	not what happens post-squash:
192	
193	- **Run the acceptance check** the Preparation stated, and
194	  record what it showed in the block, whether or not it
195	  passed. A check that was never run is a failed close-out,
196	  and a check that failed is a finding, not a reason to
197	  quietly restate the banner.
198	- **Finalize the six items in place**, before the move: sync
199	  the title if the cycle's scope shifted, replace the
200	  provisional solution statement with what was actually
201	  done, drop the ladder's `(current)` / `(done)` markers
202	  since as-built implies done, and add any `####` design
203	  subsections the deliberation grew.
204	- **Move the block** into `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`,
205	  applying the four transforms in
206	  [Chores sections](#chores-sections). This *creates* the
207	  section; nothing was opened earlier.
208	- **Write the `## Done` entry**: the version, then a bold
209	  title line with its chores `[N]` ref and detail as
210	  sub-bullets (see
211	  [Done entry form](../agent-data/notes.md#done-entry-form)).
212	- **Replace the `## In Progress` block** with
213	  `_No cycle currently in progress._`.
214	- **Update `notes/README.md`** if functionality changed
215	  (new flags, new subcommands, changed behavior).
216	
217	Whether to **squash** the cycle into one commit before the
218	publishing push, or push as-is, is decided at push time;
219	see [Pushing](#pushing).
220	
221	## Step naming
222	
223	A step has a title and no number. The ladder lists its rungs in order, so position is already
224	recorded by the list, and a step is referred to by its title, verbatim-identical in the ladder
225	rung, the chores `##` header and the commit (see
226	[agent-data/prose.md](../agent-data/prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)). A title has to be
227	unambiguous within its cycle and within its chores file, where it is also an anchor; it may repeat
228	across the repo's history.
229	
230	The version-of-record still bumps for every step, and its suffix still encodes the phase, but that
231	encoding belongs to the manifest and appears nowhere in prose. It is the one number left in the
232	system, it names nothing, and nothing dereferences it. The full scheme (disambiguation, nesting,
233	optional Preparation, the project's version-of-record format, and the per-phase bump) lives in
234	[versioning.md](versioning.md#suffix-scheme), which is the single source of truth for this repo's
235	versioning.
236	
237	## Topic bookmarks are drafts
238	
239	A topic bookmark is a draft until it lands on a permanent branch. Pushing to the bookmark makes
240	the work durable and visible; it does not publish it. Landing on the permanent branch is
241	publication, and that is the line the rules divide at:
242	
243	- **Before landing**, the series should be self-consistent when practical. Inserting or
244	  reordering a step changes the ladder, and the rungs that already committed an older version of
245	  it are brought along, so the branch reads as one coherent ladder rather than a record of how it
246	  was assembled.
247	- **After landing**, the commits are history and are not touched. A recorded SHA is only ever
248	  written for a commit on a permanent branch (see [Commits backfill](#commits-backfill)), which
249	  is what makes rewriting a draft safe.
250	
251	Mechanics, and why they cost so little here:
252	
253	- **Amend content; never re-describe.** Editing `TODO.md` inside a rung and amending it is not a
254	  `jj describe`, so the never-re-describe rule stays intact. `ochid:` trailers survive, since
255	  they carry change ids rather than commit ids and a change id is stable across a rewrite.
256	- **Force-push the bookmark** afterwards, under the same approval any push needs.
257	- **Exceptions**, since "when practical" is not "always": the bookmark has already landed;
258	  another branch is stacked on it, so the rewrite becomes someone else's rebase; or the ladder is
259	  long and only a trailing snapshot disagrees. Name the reason and move on.
260	
261	A squash-form [sub-cycle ladder](#sub-cycle-ladders) never meets this, because nothing on it is
262	pushed and the close-out squash collapses it. The rule is for the multi-commit shape, whose rungs
263	publish one at a time.
264	
265	## Per-commit flow
266	
267	Every commit (Preparation, each Work commit, Close-out) goes
268	through:
269	
270	1. **Mark this commit `(current)`** as the first edit in
271	   `TODO.md > ## In Progress` (`TODO.md` is at the repo
272	   root).
273	2. **Do the work** (see [Iterative work](#iterative-work)
274	   for the loop-and-squash technique).
275	3. **Flip this commit `(current)` -> `(done)`** in `## In
276	   Progress`, before the cargo cycle and the commit.
277	4. **Validate the artifact**, a medium-specific step, skip-able
278	   for notes-only commits, mandatory at close-out. For the Rust
279	   example the cargo cycle is:
280	   1. `cargo fmt`
281	   2. `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`
282	   3. `cargo test`
283	   4. `cargo install --path . --locked`
284	   5. (re-test if anything substantive changed)
285	5. **Work review.** Stop *before* writing any description;
286	   tell the user "ready to commit." The user reviews the
287	   changes and we iterate until complete.
288	6. **Write the commit description**; see
289	   [Commit description](#commit-description).
290	7. **Commit Description review.** Show the title + body
291	   and stop. The user reviews the description. Iterate.
292	8. **Commit.** `jj commit -m "title" -m "body" -R .` for
293	   the work repo, `-R .claude` for the bot repo (`-R` last
294	   keeps the verb visible):
295	
296	   ```
297	   jj commit -m \
298	   "<type>: <short description>" \
299	   -m "<problem statement>
300	
301	   <solution statement>
302	
303	   - <a rule or outcome that followed>
304	   - <another>
305	
306	   ochid: /.claude/<chid>" \
307	   -R .
308	   ```
309	
310	**Two overrides apply:**
311	
312	- **Deviation or question**: any time the work deviates
313	  from the agreed plan, or a question arises, stop and
314	  surface it; don't push through.
315	- **ESC-ESC**: the user can interrupt at any point to pull
316	  a review or question forward.
317	
318	## Commit description
319	
320	[Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/):
321	
322	```
323	<type>: <short description>
324	```
325	
326	**A commit names no version**, in its title or its body. The version-of-record (where it lives
327	and its bump cadence, see [versioning.md](versioning.md)) is useful for confirming you are
328	running the version you are testing; it is not an identifier, and a commit already records it in
329	the manifest. Writing it into the description copies it into text that cannot be edited: a
330	version is only stable once it lands on the permanent branch, and even then a history rewrite may
331	renumber it, at which point every description naming it is wrong forever. See
332	[Versions live in the version-of-record only](../agent-data/prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only).
333	
334	### Title
335	
336	- <=50 chars total.
337	- Common types: `feat`, `fix`, `refactor`, `test`, `docs`, `chore`.
338	- Favor terse phrasings.
339	- **Distinct per step**: each of a cycle's commits gets its own descriptive title (no shared
340	  cycle title with a step marker). Share a greppable stem across the cycle's titles (e.g.
341	  `ring buffer`) so `git log --grep` collects them; the chores section header matches the
342	  close-out title.
343	- **Unambiguous where it is resolved**: the title is the only identifier a record has, so it must
344	  be distinct within its cycle and within its chores file (a `##` header is also an anchor). It
345	  may repeat across the repo's history. See
346	  [Steps are named, not numbered](../agent-data/prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered).
347	
348	### Body
349	
350	A **problem statement** then a **solution statement**, in
351	[Prose form](../agent-data/prose.md#prose-form) (intro + bullets), wrapped <=72. The problem
352	statement says what was wrong and defines any word the title assumes; the solution statement says
353	what was done about it. Content rules, including why the body carries no file list, are in
354	[agent-data/prose.md](../agent-data/prose.md#prose-form) and are not repeated here.
355	
356	Two repo-specific points:
357	
358	- **Work-repo body**: the problem is the artifact's or the records' problem.
359	- **Bot-repo (`.claude`) body**: the statements describe in-session activity rather than
360	  work-repo changes.
361	
362	### Trailer
363	
364	`ochid:` as the last line of the body; see
365	[Cross-repo linking (ochid trailers)](../AGENTS.md#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)
366	in AGENTS.md for the convention.
367	
368	For breaking changes, use the hyphenated `BREAKING-CHANGE:`
369	trailer key. `BREAKING CHANGE:` (with a space) is the only
370	space-separated key the Conventional Commits spec allows; the
371	hyphenated form is also valid and avoids the space ambiguity.
372	
373	## Reviewing changes
374	
375	Work review looks at the **uncommitted working-copy diff**,
376	on the way to commit. The user opens diffs in their
377	editor (Zed, VSCode); jj commands are for terminal:
378	
379	- `jj diff`: working-copy diff (uncommitted)
380	- `jj diff -r @-`: diff of the previous commit
381	- `jj diff --from <X> --to <Y>`: any two revisions
382	- `jj show -r <X>`: description + diff for one rev
383	
384	Don't `jj edit -r @-` to view a past commit, because that marks
385	it mutable and shifts `@`; use `jj diff -r @-` or
386	`jj show -r @-`.
387	
388	See [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders) for the
389	close-out squash recipe and recovery; revset primitives
390	are in [`jj-tips.md`](jj-tips.md#revsets).
391	
392	## Pushing
393	
394	### Policy
395	
396	Push is **discretionary** during the cycle (backup,
397	progress visibility) and **mandatory at close-out**, since
398	the cycle's result must be published.
399	
400	**Approval is per-push.** Every push (any repo, any kind:
401	cycle push, interim backup, recovery/surgery force-push)
402	happens only after the user has reviewed the changes to be
403	published and explicitly approved that specific push.
404	Approval of a plan that *includes* a push does not authorize
405	the push itself; stop and ask again at the moment of pushing.
406	
407	**Default is interactive; an explicit scoped delegation waives
408	the gates.** The gates above (per-push approval, the
409	commit-description review (show title+body and stop), and the
410	hard stop after push/squash-push) are the *interactive
411	default*.
412	They yield when the user **explicitly** delegates a complete,
413	bounded task and authorizes carrying it through ("do all of X
414	and push each step, don't check in"). The bot then proceeds
415	through that task's commits and pushes without stopping, and
416	continues past each push to the next step. Conditions:
417	
418	- **Explicit grant**: never inferred from a task merely being
419	  well-scoped; the user's words must authorize unattended
420	  completion. "Commit and push" (or "then push") names the
421	  destination, not a waiver: it authorizes the push *after*
422	  the normal work review and description review, not skipping
423	  them. Only wording that explicitly waives the stops ("don't
424	  check in", "no need to review", "carry it through
425	  unattended") waives them.
426	- **Bounded goal**: covers the named task only; does not carry
427	  to the next task or a vaguer follow-on.
428	- **Destructive ops still pause**: delegation covers the task's
429	  ordinary commits and pushes; it does *not* pre-authorize a
430	  genuinely irreversible action (force-push over published
431	  history, history rewrite, deleting a remote branch). Those can
432	  permanently destroy work and aren't a normal cycle step, so the
433	  bot flags one before acting. An ordinary delegated cycle never
434	  reaches this.
435	- **Still transparent**: report each commit/push as it lands
436	  (title + outcome) so the user can catch up.
437	- **When in doubt, ask**: ambiguous authorization falls back to
438	  per-push approval.
439	
440	### Shape at close-out push
441	
442	At close-out the cycle's *work* is done; its *published
443	shape* is the remaining choice, made at push time. Surface
444	the options and get user approval before pushing. Once on
445	the target, changing shape is a remote rewrite (force-push,
446	needs approval), so choose deliberately.
447	
448	- **Squash to one commit**: single entry on the target.
449	  Right for straightforward changes where the Work-N is
450	  focused on one or two files.
451	- **Merge non-ff** *(current default)*: `main` gains the close-out as a merge commit; cycle
452	  commits stay reachable via two parents. `jj log -r ..@ -n <N>` shows the trapezoidal shape. See
453	  [Merge non-ff recipe](#merge-non-ff-recipe) for the full setup sequence.
454	- **Keep separate**: one commit per cycle entry on
455	  `main`. Use when the decomposition itself is
456	  informative. Each chores section keeps its own header /
457	  `Commits:` ref; no consolidation churn.
458	
459	Set up squash/merge before invoking `vc-x1 push`; use
460	`jj git push` directly for non-standard shapes.
461	
462	### Merge non-ff recipe
463	
464	Setting up a [Merge non-ff](#shape-at-close-out-push)
465	close-out is a fixed sequence. `<closeout>` is the cycle's
466	close-out commit, `<prev>` the previous cycle's close-out
467	(the current `main` tip), `<work-tip>` the cycle's last
468	Work commit:
469	
470	1. **Rebase the close-out into a merge**: `jj rebase -r
471	   <closeout> --onto <prev> --onto <work-tip>`.
472	   - `-r <closeout>` keeps the `<closeout>` commit in place.
473	   - `--onto <prev>` becomes its first parent (trunk).
474	   - `--onto <work-tip>` becomes the second parent.
475	
476	   Together these make `<closeout>` a merge of
477	   `<prev>` + `<work-tip>`, forming a trapezoidal commit.
478	2. **Use `jj new <merge>`** to add an empty `@` above the
479	   merge. The rebase left `@` *on* the now-content-bearing
480	   merge, which git/IDE diff views show as uncommitted;
481	   `jj new` restores the clean empty `@` on top.
482	3. **Push**: `jj git push --bookmark main -R .`.
483	
484	**Post-hoc caveat.** If the cycle was already pushed
485	[Keep separate](#shape-at-close-out-push) its commits are
486	immutable: the rebase needs `--ignore-immutable` and the
487	push force-updates `main`.
488	The standard sequence assumes the merge is set up *before*
489	the close-out push.
490	
491	**Viewing the result (not a push step).** After merge
492	non-ff close-outs land, read the history with
493	`jj log -r ..@ -n <N>`: the graph renders each cycle as its
494	trapezoid, with close-out titles down the trunk's left edge and
495	the cycle's Work rungs indented on the side leg, so trunk and
496	internals are both visible at once. For git-side tooling
497	(which lists commits flat instead of drawing the graph),
498	`git log --first-parent` recovers the trunk view: one
499	close-out merge per cycle, rungs skipped; plain `git log`
500	interleaves every cycle's rungs into one long list.
501	
502	### vc-x1 push wrapper
503	
504	`vc-x1 push <bookmark>` wraps per-push mechanics. See
505	`vc-x1 push --help` for current flags. `<bookmark>` names a
506	work-repo bookmark only; the bot repo is always pinned to
507	`main` (see [.claude cadence](#claude-cadence)).
508	
509	**Current limitation**: only fully supports the
510	[Keep separate](#shape-at-close-out-push) shape; other
511	shapes need manual jj steps. Planned improvements are
512	project state, tracked in the project's `TODO.md`;
513	this protocol describes only the stable mechanism.
514	
515	### .claude cadence
516	
517	**Cadence**: one push = one bot-repo commit, paired
518	with every work-repo commit in that push.
519	
520	The `.claude` working copy accumulates session data
521	across the cycle; its change ID stays stable across
522	snapshots, `jj describe`, and the squash-push fold, so
523	work-repo `ochid:` trailers resolve.
524	
525	`.claude` is a linear journal: all session work lives
526	on `main`, regardless of the work-repo bookmark. **Do
527	not create or maintain bot-repo bookmarks that mirror
528	work-repo branches**, which risks the bot steering session
529	pushes to the wrong remote ref.
530	
531	Ending a session: if the user runs `/exit` there will be
532	session information created, which we don't worry about.
533	The user can close the terminal instead and `@` will
534	remain empty.
535	
536	### Bot communication at the reviews
537	
538	Use plain prose, no insider jargon ("Gate N signal",
539	"Checkpoint N", etc.):
540	
541	- **At Work review**: summarize what changed and stop.
542	  "Work complete. Please review."
543	- **At Commit Description review**: present `$TITLE`
544	  and `$BODY` explicitly; ask permission to commit/push.
545	  Don't spell out the full `vc-x1 push ... --title ...
546	  --body ...` invocation by default.
547	- **At Post close-out review**: surface the shape
548	  options (squash / merge / keep) and the push target;
549	  wait for the user's choice before any `jj squash` /
550	  `jj rebase` / `jj git push` invocation.
551	
552	### After push or squash-push: stop and wait
553	
554	After a **push** (crossing the remote boundary, by hand or
555	via the `vc-x1 push` wrapper, whose last stage publishes
556	the bot repo too) or a manual **squash-push** on the bot
557	repo, stop for the turn: no next step, edit, tool call, or
558	text output until the user directs otherwise. **Even when
559	the next step seems obvious, wait.**
560	
561	- **Scope**: the stop follows the user's directive, not the
562	  push. A standing directive covering more work ("finish
563	  the remaining ladder commits on your own") makes an
564	  intermediate push just a step; the hard stop lands on the
565	  turn's *final* push.
566	- **Why**: the bot repo is a live journal, so everything after
567	  the invocation (its own record, closing words) lands in
568	  `@` as a trailing tail. Between delegated pushes the tail
569	  rides into the next cycle's bot commit; the final push's
570	  tail has no next commit, and the bot's own squash-push is
571	  itself session data (`@` refills immediately), so only the
572	  user, after the turn, can capture it
573	  (`vc-x1 squash-push -R .claude`).
574	- **Silence**: put all closing words *before* the final
575	  push. The harness rejects an empty turn, so it may force a
576	  visible token after the tool returns; if so, emit a bare
577	  acknowledgment only (e.g. "landed"), never a summary,
578	  verification, or next-step offer. There is no "harmless"
579	  closing line after the push; that is a known slip.
580	- **Flush**: when the user wants `@` empty (no tail), they
581	  run `vc-x1 squash-push -R .claude` after the bot goes
582	  quiet. It flushes all bot session information into the
583	  published commit. Repeat if new writes land (see
584	  [Recovery](#recovery)).
585	
586	### Recovery
587	
588	- **If push exits before its last stage**, meaning `push-work`
589	  succeeded but the bot-repo publish didn't run
590	  (`squash-push-bot` in `vc-x1 push --status` / `--from`
591	  stage names), run the squash+push by hand:
592	
593	  ```
594	  vc-x1 squash-push -R .claude
595	  ```
596	
597	  It runs in-process, so a failure is a visible non-zero
598	  exit, with no log file to chase.
599	- **Run squash-push again if `@` is non-empty** after a
600	  pass (also desirable after extra activity by the bot's
601	  agents).
602	  - Why: the bot keeps writing session data while the
603	    command runs: the invocation's own record plus any
604	    closing response land after the squash.
605	  - Safe to repeat: bot session data is append-only, so a
606	    re-run never conflicts or overwrites. (This could
607	    change; it is not under the user's control.)
608	  - No guarantees: events outside the bot's control can leave
609	    `@` non-empty. The bot's back end may decide to
610	    squash/consolidate session data, which can take minutes
611	    and land after the pass. The remedy is the same: just
612	    run squash-push again. This is why a single pass is never
613	    guaranteed to leave `@` empty.
614	- **Clear push's saved state** after any out-of-band
615	  recovery, via `rm .vc-x1/push-state.toml` or `vc-x1 push
616	  <bookmark> --restart`; otherwise push resumes from a
617	  stale stage.
618	- **Late work-repo tweak after the work-repo push succeeded**
619	  (e.g. updating AGENTS.md or memory) requires `jj
620	  squash --ignore-immutable` and a re-push; that is a
621	  remote rewrite and needs explicit approval like any
622	  push.
623	- **`vc-x1 push` after a manual merge setup published an
624	  empty commit** (seen at the 0.22.0 close-out). `vc-x1
625	  push` *creates* the work commit itself from pending
626	  changes + `--title`/`--body`; it does not publish an
627	  already-committed shape. Invoked after the
628	  [Merge non-ff recipe](#merge-non-ff-recipe) (work repo
629	  clean, merge in place), it minted an **empty** commit on
630	  the old `main` tip, stamped the ochid on it, and pushed
631	  that, leaving the merge unreferenced and `main` without
632	  the cycle's content. Prevention: after a manual shape
633	  setup, push with `jj git push --bookmark main -R .`
634	  directly (the recipe's step 3), never `vc-x1 push`.
635	  Recovery, in order (nothing is lost, the merge still
636	  exists):
637	  1. `jj describe <merge>` to append the
638	     `ochid: /.claude/<bot-chid>` trailer the stray got
639	     instead (rewrites the merge's commit id; its chid,
640	     what the bot side references, is stable).
641	  2. `jj abandon <stray> --ignore-immutable`.
642	  3. `jj bookmark set main -r <merge> --allow-backwards`,
643	     `jj new <merge>`, then `jj git push --bookmark main
644	     -R .` (remote rewrite, needs approval).
645	  4. Bot repo: `jj describe <bot-commit> --ignore-immutable
646	     -R .claude` to point its `ochid:` at the merge's chid,
647	     then `jj git push --bookmark main -R .claude`
648	     (restores the `main == main@origin` preflight
649	     invariant).
650	
651	  The recovered shape, `jj log -r ..@` (0.22.0, elided):
652	
653	  ```
654	  @  smpozlop ... (empty) (no description set)
655	  ◆    yzvlvtku ... main d9bb5882
656	  ├─╮  fix: calibration robust to codegen and noise
657	  │ ◆  ztxvxuru ... fix-calibration f4b155a8
658	  │ │  feat: always-on calibration self-checks
659	  │ ~  (three more rungs)
660	  │ ◆  tskxkxsk ... 6d5784de
661	  ├─╯  fix: pair frame/call against a loop-only pass
662	  ◆  sktyvwrq ... f006b09e
663	  │  feat: amortized + cached calibration
664	  ```
665	
666	## Iterative work
667	
668	When work for a single commit (the **target**) benefits
669	from incremental review, loop:
670	
671	1. `jj new -R .`: fresh empty `@` on top of the target.
672	2. Make the next round of changes.
673	3. User reviews the round (see
674	   [Reviewing changes](#reviewing-changes)).
675	4. `jj squash -R .` folds into the target and creates a
676	   new empty `@`.
677	5. If not done, go to step 2.
678	
679	Same jj mechanics as a
680	[sub-cycle ladder](#sub-cycle-ladders), but at
681	single-commit scope, so the version
682	doesn't change.
683	
684	## Sub-cycle ladders
685	
686	When a Work commit subdivides into a sub-cycle (see
687	[Step naming](#step-naming), and [versioning.md](versioning.md#suffix-scheme) for how the
688	manifest's suffix nests), its Work
689	commits typically live as a local jj `@` chain and
690	**collapse into the sub-cycle's Close-out** before the
691	parent cycle continues. Ladder commits are scratch,
692	for review and bisection only.
693	
694	### Per-Work-commit contract within a ladder
695	
696	For each Work commit in the ladder:
697	
698	1. `jj new -R .`: create a fresh empty `@`.
699	2. Do the commit's work.
700	3. Run the fast validation (Rust example: `cargo test
701	   --bins`). **Non-negotiable**: for code, build and clippy
702	   alone miss regressions until a later commit runs the full
703	   suite, raising bisection cost.
704	4. `jj describe -m "..." -m "..." -R .`: working title
705	   only; the sub-cycle Close-out collects everything
706	   into one final commit.
707	
708	### Navigating the ladder
709	
710	Common moves:
711	
712	- `jj log -r '<base>::' -R .`: see the whole ladder
713	  from its base.
714	- `jj edit -r <prefix> -R .`: jump `@` to any ladder
715	  commit by chid prefix; useful for bisection.
716	- `jj edit @-- -R .`: quick-jump back two commits.
717	- `jj diff -r <chid> -R .`: review one commit in
718	  isolation.
719	
720	Modifications to any ladder commit rewrite it in place;
721	descendants auto-rebase.
722	
723	### Close-out: squash the ladder
724	
725	When all ladder Work commits are done and tests pass:
726	
727	```
728	jj squash --from "<base>..@-" --into @ -u -R .
729	```
730	
731	`<base>` is the parent of the first ladder commit; `-u`
732	keeps `@`'s description and discards the sources'.
733	After squash, history is linear: `<base> -> @`;
734	intermediate commits are auto-abandoned.
735	
736	Then `vc-x1 push <bookmark>` as for any other commit.
737	
738	For N = 1 the squash is a no-op (`<base>..@-` is empty
739	when `@-` is `<base>`); push the single commit directly.
740	
741	### Recovery
742	
743	If a ladder commit goes wrong, back out without losing
744	prior commits:
745	
746	- **Discard the current commit.** `jj abandon @ -R .`
747	  drops it; you get a fresh empty `@` on the same
748	  parent.
749	- **Edit an earlier commit.** `jj edit -r <chid> -R .`,
750	  make corrections, then `jj edit -r <last-ladder-chid>`
751	  to return. Descendants auto-rebase.
752	- **Discard the entire ladder.** `jj op log -R .` shows
753	  the op history; `jj op restore <op-id> -R .` reverts
754	  to that point. Full undo: removes *all* ladder work
755	  after the chosen op. Use only to start over.
756	
757	# References
758	
759	- [`jj-tips.md`](jj-tips.md#revsets): revset primitives
760	  (chid/cid, `@`/`@-`/`@+`, `..`/`::` ranges, prefix matching).
761	- The per-commit `cargo test --bins` gate exists because a
762	  regression introduced in an early ladder commit can go
763	  uncaught until a later commit runs the full suite, raising
764	  bisection cost.
765

# Cycle protocol

This protocol uses [Prose form](../agent-data/prose.md#prose-form). It
contains instructions on how a commit cycle is accomplished.

The artifact a cycle produces is whatever the bot generates from
the conversation: code, prose, an image, a song, a screenplay.
The steps below use a Rust crate as the running example (the
cargo cycle, `Cargo.toml` versioning); substitute your medium's
equivalents. This project's manifest is recorded in
[versioning.md](versioning.md).

## Cycles

A cycle has three phases:

- **[Preparation](#preparation)**: the cycle's first commit, when it needs setup (a lightweight
  cycle omits it and starts at its first Work step). Sets up the cycle:
  - Bump the version-of-record (where it lives and the suffix scheme are project-specific; see
    [versioning.md](versioning.md)).
  - Pick up a `## Todo` item (typically the top-ranked, #1)
    into `## In Progress` as the cycle's
    [six provisional items](#preparation): title, problem
    statement, solution statement, acceptance check, ladder,
    deliberation.
  - Create the cycle's topic bookmark.
  - Nothing is opened in the chores file; the block is the
    cycle's only home until close-out moves it.
- **[Work-N](#work-n)**: the commits that implement the change. As many as the change needs;
  each runs through the [per-commit flow](#per-commit-flow).
- **[Close-out](#close-out)**: the cycle's last commit. Bookkeeping only:
  - Run the acceptance check and record what it showed.
  - Finalize the six items, then move the block into
    `notes/chores/`, which creates the
    [chores section](#chores-sections).
  - Write the `## Done` entry and clear `## In Progress`.
  - Land the cycle's bookmark.
  - Optionally update `notes/README.md` if functionality
    changed.

A cycle's commits are published to the project remote
either incrementally or as one batch at close-out; the
result must always be published at close-out. See
[Pushing](#pushing).

**Sub-cycles.** When a Work commit's scope grows enough to warrant its own ladder, it subdivides
into its own Preparation / Work / Close-out. The same three-phase shape applies recursively at
every depth, and a sub-ladder's rungs are titles like any other. See
[Step naming](#step-naming) for how a step is identified and
[Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders) for the local-ladder mechanics.

## Chores sections

A **chores section** is a `##` section in
`notes/chores/chores-NN.md` recording landed work. In
general, every commit that lands on the permanent branch
should have a reference to it on a rung of its section's
as-built ladder in a chores file.

**A cycle's record has one home at a time.** While the cycle
runs it lives entirely in `TODO.md > ## In Progress`, as the
[six provisional items](#preparation) written at Preparation
and revised as steps land. At close-out the whole block
**moves** into the chores file, becoming that cycle's `##`
section. It is never written in two places, so there is
nothing to keep in sync and nothing to write twice.

The move is mechanical, four transforms and no rewriting:

- **Heading levels shift one deeper**: the block's `###`
  title becomes the section's `##`, and its `####` items
  become `###`. Anchors survive untouched, because GitHub
  slugs derive from the heading's *text*, not its level.
- **Rung refs renumber** into the destination file's `[N]`
  namespace (see [Reference numbering](../agent-data/notes.md#reference-numbering)).
- **Repo-root-relative links gain `../`**, since the block
  moves from the root into `notes/chores/`.
- **The block's own forward-looking notes are rewritten**,
  since they described a future that has now happened.

Two of those fail *silently*: a mis-renumbered ref and an
un-rebased link render as plain text or a 404 rather than
erroring. Check both by hand until a `validate-repo` exists.

A single-commit cycle's ladder is one rung, its close-out.
Rung placeholders are backfilled once the commit is
permanent (see [Commits backfill](#commits-backfill) below).

The move also appends the section's title-only
`- [<title>](#<anchor>)` entry to the file's
`## Table of Contents`.

Adopted from vc-x1, which trialled it through a full cycle
and kept it: the dual maintenance disappeared, and the
narrative did not thin out from being written in `TODO.md`,
which was the risk.

Fuller chores conventions (content rules, header sync,
design subsection pattern, rung / reference formatting)
live in
[agent-data/notes.md](../agent-data/notes.md#chores-conventions).

### Commits backfill

An as-built ladder rung cites its commit by SHA and records the version that commit carried, and
neither is stable until the commit lands on a **permanent branch** (`main`, or a long-lived
release/patch branch that won't be rewritten); a rebase or squash rewrites the SHA and may
renumber the version on the way. So:

- A rung is **written with the literal `[[N]]` placeholder and no version**.
- **Backfill once the commit is on a permanent branch**, where both are final. A commit can't
  record its own SHA (that would change the hash), so the fill always lands one push later:
  **each push backfills the rungs of the commits the previous push made permanent.** On a topic
  branch the sections instead wait until the branch lands, so nothing is ever written that a
  later rebase could invalidate.

Backfill replaces the placeholder with a file-local `[[N]]` ref, defined as the commit URL +
40-hex SHA in the file's `# References` (format in agent-data/notes.md
[Chores commit references](../agent-data/notes.md#chores-commit-references)), and writes the
version ahead of the title. Sections predating the ladder form keep their legacy `Commits:`
lines; backfill those where they exist. A section's `##` title matches its commit title, so a
rare deliberate rewrite of a permanent-branch commit re-syncs via `git log --grep "<title>"`.

The per-push cadence is a project choice, not dogma: a **per-close-out** model (recording a
cycle's SHAs at its close-out) is equally valid. The one invariant: what a rung records must be
permanent.

## Preparation

The cycle's first commit, when the cycle needs setup (a lightweight cycle omits it; see
[versioning.md](versioning.md#suffix-scheme)):

- **Bump the version-of-record.** Where it lives, the suffix scheme, and any derived files (a
  lockfile, a sourced manifest version) are project-specific; see
  [versioning.md](versioning.md).
- **Move a `## Todo` item** (if the cycle has one) into
  `## In Progress`, and write the cycle's **six provisional
  items** there. All six are required, all six are revised
  as steps land, and all six move to chores at close-out.
  The first is a `###` heading; the rest are `####` headings
  under it:
  - the **title**, which becomes the chores section header.
  - the **problem statement**: what is wrong, in a sentence
    or two.
  - the **solution statement**: what will be done about it,
    broad. Provisional here, since it is written before the
    work; the close-out's commit body carries the final one.
  - the **acceptance check**: the measure of "are you
    finished?". Not the per-commit validation, which asks
    whether the artifact still works; this asks whether the
    thing the cycle promised actually happened, specifically
    enough that a reader can run it.
  - the **ladder**: one rung per step, a bare title plus a
    `(current)` / `(done)` marker.
  - the **deliberation**: how the five above were decided,
    alternatives weighed, costs accepted. `_None._` when
    there was nothing to deliberate, which is a real answer
    and different from having forgotten to write it.

Nothing is opened in the chores file at Preparation. The
section is created at close-out by moving this block; see
[Chores sections](#chores-sections).

**Why an acceptance check, and why it is provisional.** A
cycle's own per-commit checklists can all pass while its
banner claim is false: vc-x1's seven-cycle program opened
against "end subprocess spawning" and its close-out claimed
the goal met, with about twenty spawn sites surviving, two
inside the facade the program built. Being provisional, the
check can also be revised *toward* what was achieved, which
is the same failure by a slower route. So a changed check is
one of the things the deliberation exists to justify.

## Work-N

The cycle's work commits implement the change. As many as needed:

- Each commit runs through the
  **[per-commit flow](#per-commit-flow)**.
- **Interim pushes** are optional (backup, progress
  visibility).
- Close-out is the only mandatory push (see
  [Pushing](#pushing)).
- **Subdivide into a sub-cycle** if a Work commit's
  scope grows enough (see
  [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders)).

## Close-out

The cycle's last commit does bookkeeping only, and the commit body describes that bookkeeping,
not what happens post-squash:

- **Run the acceptance check** the Preparation stated, and
  record what it showed in the block, whether or not it
  passed. A check that was never run is a failed close-out,
  and a check that failed is a finding, not a reason to
  quietly restate the banner.
- **Finalize the six items in place**, before the move: sync
  the title if the cycle's scope shifted, replace the
  provisional solution statement with what was actually
  done, drop the ladder's `(current)` / `(done)` markers
  since as-built implies done, and add any `####` design
  subsections the deliberation grew.
- **Move the block** into `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`,
  applying the four transforms in
  [Chores sections](#chores-sections). This *creates* the
  section; nothing was opened earlier.
- **Write the `## Done` entry**: the version, then a bold
  title line with its chores `[N]` ref and detail as
  sub-bullets (see
  [Done entry form](../agent-data/notes.md#done-entry-form)).
- **Replace the `## In Progress` block** with
  `_No cycle currently in progress._`.
- **Update `notes/README.md`** if functionality changed
  (new flags, new subcommands, changed behavior).

Whether to **squash** the cycle into one commit before the
publishing push, or push as-is, is decided at push time;
see [Pushing](#pushing).

## Step naming

A step has a title and no number. The ladder lists its rungs in order, so position is already
recorded by the list, and a step is referred to by its title, verbatim-identical in the ladder
rung, the chores `##` header and the commit (see
[agent-data/prose.md](../agent-data/prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)). A title has to be
unambiguous within its cycle and within its chores file, where it is also an anchor; it may repeat
across the repo's history.

The version-of-record still bumps for every step, and its suffix still encodes the phase, but that
encoding belongs to the manifest and appears nowhere in prose. It is the one number left in the
system, it names nothing, and nothing dereferences it. The full scheme (disambiguation, nesting,
optional Preparation, the project's version-of-record format, and the per-phase bump) lives in
[versioning.md](versioning.md#suffix-scheme), which is the single source of truth for this repo's
versioning.

## Topic bookmarks are drafts

A topic bookmark is a draft until it lands on a permanent branch. Pushing to the bookmark makes
the work durable and visible; it does not publish it. Landing on the permanent branch is
publication, and that is the line the rules divide at:

- **Before landing**, the series should be self-consistent when practical. Inserting or
  reordering a step changes the ladder, and the rungs that already committed an older version of
  it are brought along, so the branch reads as one coherent ladder rather than a record of how it
  was assembled.
- **After landing**, the commits are history and are not touched. A recorded SHA is only ever
  written for a commit on a permanent branch (see [Commits backfill](#commits-backfill)), which
  is what makes rewriting a draft safe.

Mechanics, and why they cost so little here:

- **Amend content; never re-describe.** Editing `TODO.md` inside a rung and amending it is not a
  `jj describe`, so the never-re-describe rule stays intact. `ochid:` trailers survive, since
  they carry change ids rather than commit ids and a change id is stable across a rewrite.
- **Force-push the bookmark** afterwards, under the same approval any push needs.
- **Exceptions**, since "when practical" is not "always": the bookmark has already landed;
  another branch is stacked on it, so the rewrite becomes someone else's rebase; or the ladder is
  long and only a trailing snapshot disagrees. Name the reason and move on.

A squash-form [sub-cycle ladder](#sub-cycle-ladders) never meets this, because nothing on it is
pushed and the close-out squash collapses it. The rule is for the multi-commit shape, whose rungs
publish one at a time.

## Per-commit flow

Every commit (Preparation, each Work commit, Close-out) goes
through:

1. **Mark this commit `(current)`** as the first edit in
   `TODO.md > ## In Progress` (`TODO.md` is at the repo
   root).
2. **Do the work** (see [Iterative work](#iterative-work)
   for the loop-and-squash technique).
3. **Flip this commit `(current)` -> `(done)`** in `## In
   Progress`, before the cargo cycle and the commit.
4. **Validate the artifact**, a medium-specific step, skip-able
   for notes-only commits, mandatory at close-out. For the Rust
   example the cargo cycle is:
   1. `cargo fmt`
   2. `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`
   3. `cargo test`
   4. `cargo install --path . --locked`
   5. (re-test if anything substantive changed)
5. **Work review.** Stop *before* writing any description;
   tell the user "ready to commit." The user reviews the
   changes and we iterate until complete.
6. **Write the commit description**; see
   [Commit description](#commit-description).
7. **Commit Description review.** Show the title + body
   and stop. The user reviews the description. Iterate.
8. **Commit.** `jj commit -m "title" -m "body" -R .` for
   the work repo, `-R .claude` for the bot repo (`-R` last
   keeps the verb visible):

   ```
   jj commit -m \
   "<type>: <short description>" \
   -m "<problem statement>

   <solution statement>

   - <a rule or outcome that followed>
   - <another>

   ochid: /.claude/<chid>" \
   -R .
   ```

**Two overrides apply:**

- **Deviation or question**: any time the work deviates
  from the agreed plan, or a question arises, stop and
  surface it; don't push through.
- **ESC-ESC**: the user can interrupt at any point to pull
  a review or question forward.

## Commit description

[Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/):

```
<type>: <short description>
```

**A commit names no version**, in its title or its body. The version-of-record (where it lives
and its bump cadence, see [versioning.md](versioning.md)) is useful for confirming you are
running the version you are testing; it is not an identifier, and a commit already records it in
the manifest. Writing it into the description copies it into text that cannot be edited: a
version is only stable once it lands on the permanent branch, and even then a history rewrite may
renumber it, at which point every description naming it is wrong forever. See
[Versions live in the version-of-record only](../agent-data/prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only).

### Title

- <=50 chars total.
- Common types: `feat`, `fix`, `refactor`, `test`, `docs`, `chore`.
- Favor terse phrasings.
- **Distinct per step**: each of a cycle's commits gets its own descriptive title (no shared
  cycle title with a step marker). Share a greppable stem across the cycle's titles (e.g.
  `ring buffer`) so `git log --grep` collects them; the chores section header matches the
  close-out title.
- **Unambiguous where it is resolved**: the title is the only identifier a record has, so it must
  be distinct within its cycle and within its chores file (a `##` header is also an anchor). It
  may repeat across the repo's history. See
  [Steps are named, not numbered](../agent-data/prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered).

### Body

A **problem statement** then a **solution statement**, in
[Prose form](../agent-data/prose.md#prose-form) (intro + bullets), wrapped <=72. The problem
statement says what was wrong and defines any word the title assumes; the solution statement says
what was done about it. Content rules, including why the body carries no file list, are in
[agent-data/prose.md](../agent-data/prose.md#prose-form) and are not repeated here.

Two repo-specific points:

- **Work-repo body**: the problem is the artifact's or the records' problem.
- **Bot-repo (`.claude`) body**: the statements describe in-session activity rather than
  work-repo changes.

### Trailer

`ochid:` as the last line of the body; see
[Cross-repo linking (ochid trailers)](../AGENTS.md#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)
in AGENTS.md for the convention.

For breaking changes, use the hyphenated `BREAKING-CHANGE:`
trailer key. `BREAKING CHANGE:` (with a space) is the only
space-separated key the Conventional Commits spec allows; the
hyphenated form is also valid and avoids the space ambiguity.

## Reviewing changes

Work review looks at the **uncommitted working-copy diff**,
on the way to commit. The user opens diffs in their
editor (Zed, VSCode); jj commands are for terminal:

- `jj diff`: working-copy diff (uncommitted)
- `jj diff -r @-`: diff of the previous commit
- `jj diff --from <X> --to <Y>`: any two revisions
- `jj show -r <X>`: description + diff for one rev

Don't `jj edit -r @-` to view a past commit, because that marks
it mutable and shifts `@`; use `jj diff -r @-` or
`jj show -r @-`.

See [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders) for the
close-out squash recipe and recovery; revset primitives
are in [`jj-tips.md`](jj-tips.md#revsets).

## Pushing

### Policy

Push is **discretionary** during the cycle (backup,
progress visibility) and **mandatory at close-out**, since
the cycle's result must be published.

**Approval is per-push.** Every push (any repo, any kind:
cycle push, interim backup, recovery/surgery force-push)
happens only after the user has reviewed the changes to be
published and explicitly approved that specific push.
Approval of a plan that *includes* a push does not authorize
the push itself; stop and ask again at the moment of pushing.

**Default is interactive; an explicit scoped delegation waives
the gates.** The gates above (per-push approval, the
commit-description review (show title+body and stop), and the
hard stop after push/squash-push) are the *interactive
default*.
They yield when the user **explicitly** delegates a complete,
bounded task and authorizes carrying it through ("do all of X
and push each step, don't check in"). The bot then proceeds
through that task's commits and pushes without stopping, and
continues past each push to the next step. Conditions:

- **Explicit grant**: never inferred from a task merely being
  well-scoped; the user's words must authorize unattended
  completion. "Commit and push" (or "then push") names the
  destination, not a waiver: it authorizes the push *after*
  the normal work review and description review, not skipping
  them. Only wording that explicitly waives the stops ("don't
  check in", "no need to review", "carry it through
  unattended") waives them.
- **Bounded goal**: covers the named task only; does not carry
  to the next task or a vaguer follow-on.
- **Destructive ops still pause**: delegation covers the task's
  ordinary commits and pushes; it does *not* pre-authorize a
  genuinely irreversible action (force-push over published
  history, history rewrite, deleting a remote branch). Those can
  permanently destroy work and aren't a normal cycle step, so the
  bot flags one before acting. An ordinary delegated cycle never
  reaches this.
- **Still transparent**: report each commit/push as it lands
  (title + outcome) so the user can catch up.
- **When in doubt, ask**: ambiguous authorization falls back to
  per-push approval.

### Shape at close-out push

At close-out the cycle's *work* is done; its *published
shape* is the remaining choice, made at push time. Surface
the options and get user approval before pushing. Once on
the target, changing shape is a remote rewrite (force-push,
needs approval), so choose deliberately.

- **Squash to one commit**: single entry on the target.
  Right for straightforward changes where the Work-N is
  focused on one or two files.
- **Merge non-ff** *(current default)*: `main` gains the close-out as a merge commit; cycle
  commits stay reachable via two parents. `jj log -r ..@ -n <N>` shows the trapezoidal shape. See
  [Merge non-ff recipe](#merge-non-ff-recipe) for the full setup sequence.
- **Keep separate**: one commit per cycle entry on
  `main`. Use when the decomposition itself is
  informative. Each chores section keeps its own header /
  `Commits:` ref; no consolidation churn.

Set up squash/merge before invoking `vc-x1 push`; use
`jj git push` directly for non-standard shapes.

### Merge non-ff recipe

Setting up a [Merge non-ff](#shape-at-close-out-push)
close-out is a fixed sequence. `<closeout>` is the cycle's
close-out commit, `<prev>` the previous cycle's close-out
(the current `main` tip), `<work-tip>` the cycle's last
Work commit:

1. **Rebase the close-out into a merge**: `jj rebase -r
   <closeout> --onto <prev> --onto <work-tip>`.
   - `-r <closeout>` keeps the `<closeout>` commit in place.
   - `--onto <prev>` becomes its first parent (trunk).
   - `--onto <work-tip>` becomes the second parent.

   Together these make `<closeout>` a merge of
   `<prev>` + `<work-tip>`, forming a trapezoidal commit.
2. **Use `jj new <merge>`** to add an empty `@` above the
   merge. The rebase left `@` *on* the now-content-bearing
   merge, which git/IDE diff views show as uncommitted;
   `jj new` restores the clean empty `@` on top.
3. **Push**: `jj git push --bookmark main -R .`.

**Post-hoc caveat.** If the cycle was already pushed
[Keep separate](#shape-at-close-out-push) its commits are
immutable: the rebase needs `--ignore-immutable` and the
push force-updates `main`.
The standard sequence assumes the merge is set up *before*
the close-out push.

**Viewing the result (not a push step).** After merge
non-ff close-outs land, read the history with
`jj log -r ..@ -n <N>`: the graph renders each cycle as its
trapezoid, with close-out titles down the trunk's left edge and
the cycle's Work rungs indented on the side leg, so trunk and
internals are both visible at once. For git-side tooling
(which lists commits flat instead of drawing the graph),
`git log --first-parent` recovers the trunk view: one
close-out merge per cycle, rungs skipped; plain `git log`
interleaves every cycle's rungs into one long list.

### vc-x1 push wrapper

`vc-x1 push <bookmark>` wraps per-push mechanics. See
`vc-x1 push --help` for current flags. `<bookmark>` names a
work-repo bookmark only; the bot repo is always pinned to
`main` (see [.claude cadence](#claude-cadence)).

**Current limitation**: only fully supports the
[Keep separate](#shape-at-close-out-push) shape; other
shapes need manual jj steps. Planned improvements are
project state, tracked in the project's `TODO.md`;
this protocol describes only the stable mechanism.

### .claude cadence

**Cadence**: one push = one bot-repo commit, paired
with every work-repo commit in that push.

The `.claude` working copy accumulates session data
across the cycle; its change ID stays stable across
snapshots, `jj describe`, and the squash-push fold, so
work-repo `ochid:` trailers resolve.

`.claude` is a linear journal: all session work lives
on `main`, regardless of the work-repo bookmark. **Do
not create or maintain bot-repo bookmarks that mirror
work-repo branches**, which risks the bot steering session
pushes to the wrong remote ref.

Ending a session: if the user runs `/exit` there will be
session information created, which we don't worry about.
The user can close the terminal instead and `@` will
remain empty.

### Bot communication at the reviews

Use plain prose, no insider jargon ("Gate N signal",
"Checkpoint N", etc.):

- **At Work review**: summarize what changed and stop.
  "Work complete. Please review."
- **At Commit Description review**: present `$TITLE`
  and `$BODY` explicitly; ask permission to commit/push.
  Don't spell out the full `vc-x1 push ... --title ...
  --body ...` invocation by default.
- **At Post close-out review**: surface the shape
  options (squash / merge / keep) and the push target;
  wait for the user's choice before any `jj squash` /
  `jj rebase` / `jj git push` invocation.

### After push or squash-push: stop and wait

After a **push** (crossing the remote boundary, by hand or
via the `vc-x1 push` wrapper, whose last stage publishes
the bot repo too) or a manual **squash-push** on the bot
repo, stop for the turn: no next step, edit, tool call, or
text output until the user directs otherwise. **Even when
the next step seems obvious, wait.**

- **Scope**: the stop follows the user's directive, not the
  push. A standing directive covering more work ("finish
  the remaining ladder commits on your own") makes an
  intermediate push just a step; the hard stop lands on the
  turn's *final* push.
- **Why**: the bot repo is a live journal, so everything after
  the invocation (its own record, closing words) lands in
  `@` as a trailing tail. Between delegated pushes the tail
  rides into the next cycle's bot commit; the final push's
  tail has no next commit, and the bot's own squash-push is
  itself session data (`@` refills immediately), so only the
  user, after the turn, can capture it
  (`vc-x1 squash-push -R .claude`).
- **Silence**: put all closing words *before* the final
  push. The harness rejects an empty turn, so it may force a
  visible token after the tool returns; if so, emit a bare
  acknowledgment only (e.g. "landed"), never a summary,
  verification, or next-step offer. There is no "harmless"
  closing line after the push; that is a known slip.
- **Flush**: when the user wants `@` empty (no tail), they
  run `vc-x1 squash-push -R .claude` after the bot goes
  quiet. It flushes all bot session information into the
  published commit. Repeat if new writes land (see
  [Recovery](#recovery)).

### Recovery

- **If push exits before its last stage**, meaning `push-work`
  succeeded but the bot-repo publish didn't run
  (`squash-push-bot` in `vc-x1 push --status` / `--from`
  stage names), run the squash+push by hand:

  ```
  vc-x1 squash-push -R .claude
  ```

  It runs in-process, so a failure is a visible non-zero
  exit, with no log file to chase.
- **Run squash-push again if `@` is non-empty** after a
  pass (also desirable after extra activity by the bot's
  agents).
  - Why: the bot keeps writing session data while the
    command runs: the invocation's own record plus any
    closing response land after the squash.
  - Safe to repeat: bot session data is append-only, so a
    re-run never conflicts or overwrites. (This could
    change; it is not under the user's control.)
  - No guarantees: events outside the bot's control can leave
    `@` non-empty. The bot's back end may decide to
    squash/consolidate session data, which can take minutes
    and land after the pass. The remedy is the same: just
    run squash-push again. This is why a single pass is never
    guaranteed to leave `@` empty.
- **Clear push's saved state** after any out-of-band
  recovery, via `rm .vc-x1/push-state.toml` or `vc-x1 push
  <bookmark> --restart`; otherwise push resumes from a
  stale stage.
- **Late work-repo tweak after the work-repo push succeeded**
  (e.g. updating AGENTS.md or memory) requires `jj
  squash --ignore-immutable` and a re-push; that is a
  remote rewrite and needs explicit approval like any
  push.
- **`vc-x1 push` after a manual merge setup published an
  empty commit** (seen at the 0.22.0 close-out). `vc-x1
  push` *creates* the work commit itself from pending
  changes + `--title`/`--body`; it does not publish an
  already-committed shape. Invoked after the
  [Merge non-ff recipe](#merge-non-ff-recipe) (work repo
  clean, merge in place), it minted an **empty** commit on
  the old `main` tip, stamped the ochid on it, and pushed
  that, leaving the merge unreferenced and `main` without
  the cycle's content. Prevention: after a manual shape
  setup, push with `jj git push --bookmark main -R .`
  directly (the recipe's step 3), never `vc-x1 push`.
  Recovery, in order (nothing is lost, the merge still
  exists):
  1. `jj describe <merge>` to append the
     `ochid: /.claude/<bot-chid>` trailer the stray got
     instead (rewrites the merge's commit id; its chid,
     what the bot side references, is stable).
  2. `jj abandon <stray> --ignore-immutable`.
  3. `jj bookmark set main -r <merge> --allow-backwards`,
     `jj new <merge>`, then `jj git push --bookmark main
     -R .` (remote rewrite, needs approval).
  4. Bot repo: `jj describe <bot-commit> --ignore-immutable
     -R .claude` to point its `ochid:` at the merge's chid,
     then `jj git push --bookmark main -R .claude`
     (restores the `main == main@origin` preflight
     invariant).

  The recovered shape, `jj log -r ..@` (0.22.0, elided):

  ```
  @  smpozlop ... (empty) (no description set)
  ◆    yzvlvtku ... main d9bb5882
  ├─╮  fix: calibration robust to codegen and noise
  │ ◆  ztxvxuru ... fix-calibration f4b155a8
  │ │  feat: always-on calibration self-checks
  │ ~  (three more rungs)
  │ ◆  tskxkxsk ... 6d5784de
  ├─╯  fix: pair frame/call against a loop-only pass
  ◆  sktyvwrq ... f006b09e
  │  feat: amortized + cached calibration
  ```

## Iterative work

When work for a single commit (the **target**) benefits
from incremental review, loop:

1. `jj new -R .`: fresh empty `@` on top of the target.
2. Make the next round of changes.
3. User reviews the round (see
   [Reviewing changes](#reviewing-changes)).
4. `jj squash -R .` folds into the target and creates a
   new empty `@`.
5. If not done, go to step 2.

Same jj mechanics as a
[sub-cycle ladder](#sub-cycle-ladders), but at
single-commit scope, so the version
doesn't change.

## Sub-cycle ladders

When a Work commit subdivides into a sub-cycle (see
[Step naming](#step-naming), and [versioning.md](versioning.md#suffix-scheme) for how the
manifest's suffix nests), its Work
commits typically live as a local jj `@` chain and
**collapse into the sub-cycle's Close-out** before the
parent cycle continues. Ladder commits are scratch,
for review and bisection only.

### Per-Work-commit contract within a ladder

For each Work commit in the ladder:

1. `jj new -R .`: create a fresh empty `@`.
2. Do the commit's work.
3. Run the fast validation (Rust example: `cargo test
   --bins`). **Non-negotiable**: for code, build and clippy
   alone miss regressions until a later commit runs the full
   suite, raising bisection cost.
4. `jj describe -m "..." -m "..." -R .`: working title
   only; the sub-cycle Close-out collects everything
   into one final commit.

### Navigating the ladder

Common moves:

- `jj log -r '<base>::' -R .`: see the whole ladder
  from its base.
- `jj edit -r <prefix> -R .`: jump `@` to any ladder
  commit by chid prefix; useful for bisection.
- `jj edit @-- -R .`: quick-jump back two commits.
- `jj diff -r <chid> -R .`: review one commit in
  isolation.

Modifications to any ladder commit rewrite it in place;
descendants auto-rebase.

### Close-out: squash the ladder

When all ladder Work commits are done and tests pass:

```
jj squash --from "<base>..@-" --into @ -u -R .
```

`<base>` is the parent of the first ladder commit; `-u`
keeps `@`'s description and discards the sources'.
After squash, history is linear: `<base> -> @`;
intermediate commits are auto-abandoned.

Then `vc-x1 push <bookmark>` as for any other commit.

For N = 1 the squash is a no-op (`<base>..@-` is empty
when `@-` is `<base>`); push the single commit directly.

### Recovery

If a ladder commit goes wrong, back out without losing
prior commits:

- **Discard the current commit.** `jj abandon @ -R .`
  drops it; you get a fresh empty `@` on the same
  parent.
- **Edit an earlier commit.** `jj edit -r <chid> -R .`,
  make corrections, then `jj edit -r <last-ladder-chid>`
  to return. Descendants auto-rebase.
- **Discard the entire ladder.** `jj op log -R .` shows
  the op history; `jj op restore <op-id> -R .` reverts
  to that point. Full undo: removes *all* ladder work
  after the chosen op. Use only to start over.

# References

- [`jj-tips.md`](jj-tips.md#revsets): revset primitives
  (chid/cid, `@`/`@-`/`@+`, `..`/`::` ranges, prefix matching).
- The per-commit `cargo test --bins` gate exists because a
  regression introduced in an early ladder commit can go
  uncaught until a later commit runs the full suite, raising
  bisection cost.

1	# Prose and durable text
2	
3	How long-lived text is written on this project: the prose shape, the punctuation rules, and the
4	commit-title identity. Read this before writing durable text (notes files, commit messages, doc
5	comments, chores sections).
6	
7	Universal file, pinned to the template repository; do not edit here. Project overrides go in
8	[custom.md](../custom.md).
9	
10	## Prose form
11	
12	Long-lived prose on this project follows one basic shape: a short intro that explains the *why*
13	or the high-level *what*, then a `-` bullet list for the details. Wrap lines at <=100 cols,
14	commit titles and bodies at <=72 (bullet continuations indent two spaces); existing text
15	re-wraps when touched, no mass sweeps. Write to the full width: wrap near the limit rather than
16	imitating the narrow wrap of older text. A default, not an absolute: a line that reads better
17	long stays long (an URL, a literal report row, indented code in a comment). One fact per bullet
18	or sub-bullet beats a paragraph packing several. Avoid wall-of-prose paragraphs: they hide the
19	structure that bullets make scannable. Punctuation that joins clauses without naming their relationship is
20	the same failure at sentence scale; see [Semicolons inside bullets](#semicolons-inside-bullets)
21	and [Typeable punctuation only](#typeable-punctuation-only).
22	
23	Surfaces that use this shape:
24	
25	- Module / function / struct / field doc comments in `.rs` files; see
26	  [Doc comments](code.md#doc-comments-on-every-file-function-and-method).
27	- Commit message bodies (both work-repo and bot-repo). The <=72-col title is the
28	  commit-specific add-on; see [Per-commit flow](cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow).
29	- Chore descriptions in `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`; see
30	  [Chores section content](notes.md#chores-section-content-no-edit-list-git-is-the-record).
31	- Todo and Done entries in `TODO.md` when an entry needs more than one line of detail. Pure
32	  one-liners are still fine.
33	
34	Bullet *content* differs by surface:
35	
36	- **Commit bodies**: bullets are file-by-file, one bullet per file changed, file plus a
37	  one-line gist (e.g. `README.md: new Overview intro`), detail as sub-bullets in short sentence
38	  fragments (full sentences are discouraged). Source of truth for the mechanical edit list.
39	- **Chores / todo / done**: bullets are conceptual (design points, structural notes, the "what
40	  landed and why" at a notch above file-list granularity). Never a copy of the commit's edit
41	  list; see
42	  [Chores section content](notes.md#chores-section-content-no-edit-list-git-is-the-record).
43	- **Doc comments**: bullets are whatever structure fits (fields, cases, invariants).
44	
45	### Problem + plan shape
46	
47	`## In Progress` cycle blocks, chores section intros, and `## Todo` entries use a sharper form
48	of the same shape:
49	
50	- **Problem statement** (the why): one or two sentences; don't pad with intent, don't restate
51	  the plan.
52	- **Plan bullets** (the what/when): formality differs by surface:
53	  - In Progress / chores: a committed ladder, one step per commit; see
54	    [Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) for the
55	    per-step title + `(current)` / `(done)` form.
56	  - Todo entries: rough informal bullets, no numbering; formalized only when the entry is
57	    picked up into a cycle.
58	
59	### Semicolons inside bullets
60	
61	A bullet that joins multiple clauses with semicolons (`A; B; C`) is a list hiding inside
62	running prose: break the clauses into sub-bullets so the structure shows. Semicolons in running
63	prose (intro paragraphs, sentence-joins) are fine. Not absolute: very short clauses or tight
64	pairs can stay joined inside a bullet when breaking would be more noise than signal.
65	
66	### Typeable punctuation only
67	
68	Durable text uses punctuation that can be typed at a terminal. The prohibition is on
69	*authoring*, not presence: a file may legitimately hold a banned character it transcribed (see
70	below), so a byte scan is not the rule and a sweep needs the authored/transcribed judgment.
71	Banned from authoring: `—`, `–`, `…`, `→`. None can be entered without a compose key or a paste, so none can be grepped for, and an em
72	dash next to option syntax reads as another flag. Unlike the semicolon rule above this one is
73	absolute: they cost nothing to write and are paid on every read, so a soft rule accumulates
74	them.
75	
76	`…` becomes `...` and `→` becomes `->`. The dashes have no single replacement, because an em
77	dash usually stands in for a structural decision that was not made. Make the decision:
78	
79	- **A bullet's title and its body sharing a line** is a heading and a paragraph. Make the body
80	  sub-bullets.
81	- **A term and its definition** (`jj diff`, `<base>`, a flag) takes a colon, which keeps a
82	  glossary or a command list at one line per entry.
83	- **A prose aside** takes a comma, parentheses, or two sentences. Often the aside should just
84	  go.
85	
86	Converting a heading moves its anchor. The em dash strips but the spaces on both sides survive,
87	so `## A — B` slugs to `#a--b` while its colon form slugs to `#a-b` (see
88	[Markdown anchor links](notes.md#markdown-anchor-links)). Re-point inbound links in the same
89	commit.
90	
91	Scope is the same as [Speculation marker](#speculation-marker), plus commit titles and
92	everything under `src/`: doc comments, inline comments, and any user-visible string. Source is
93	the surface a human edits and greps most, so an untypeable character costs more there than in
94	prose. It applies going forward; existing text converts when touched. A code span is not exempt
95	by itself. Naming the character is a specimen and stays, which is how this section names them.
96	A banned character doing a job is a use and converts: `` `.expect(…)` `` becomes
97	`` `.expect(...)` ``.
98	
99	Text quoted from outside this repo's prose (tool output, an error message, an already-published
100	commit title) is transcribed, not written, so it keeps its characters, whether or not it sits
101	in a code span. It matters most for commit titles: converting one stops it matching
102	`git log --grep` and breaks the verbatim identity that
103	[Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) requires between
104	a commit title, its chores header, and its `## Done` entry.
105	
106	### Conventional-commit shape (ladder / chores / commit)
107	
108	A ladder step, its chores section, and its commit description share a *title* shape, a
109	[Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/) title (`<type>: <desc>`,
110	an optional `(scope)` after the type: `feat(push): ...`) over [Prose form](#prose-form) detail.
111	They differ in the title's prefix / marker (below) and in bullet *content*: commit bodies are
112	file-by-file, ladder / chores conceptual (see "Bullet *content* differs by surface" above). The
113	shared template:
114	
115	```
116	<optional - X.Y.Z[-N]> <title>   # <title> is the commit's `<type>: <desc>`
